evidence.snippet: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a hematological malignancy driven by a chimeric oncoprotein containing the C terminus of the retinoic acid receptor-a (RARa) fused to an N-terminal partner, most commonly promyelocytic leukemia protein (PML).
evidence.explanation: The review identifies PML-RARa as the driver oncoprotein in APL.

evidence.snippet: In about 10% of the cases, a successful cytogenetic analysis may lack classic t(15;17). In the majority of such cases, a molecular analysis nevertheless reveals an underlying PML–RARA fusion transcript formed as a result of cytogenetically cryptic or complex insertion events
evidence.explanation: The review establishes that cryptic or complex events can produce PML-RARA without a visible classic translocation.

steps/3.description: An acquired rearrangement fuses PML with RARA in a myeloid progenitor. Most cases have the classic t(15;17), but cryptic or complex insertions can generate the same fusion transcript without a visible classic translocation. PML::RARA is the initiating driver of this disease entry, while model studies show that additional events influence progression from a preleukemic state to overt leukemia.

evidence.snippet: It binds to retinoic acid response elements of target genes and recruits co-repressors such as DNA methyltransferases and histone deacetylases
evidence.explanation: The review describes the corepressor and chromatin-repressor complex recruited by PML::RARA.

steps/4.description: PML::RARA binds retinoic-acid response elements and recruits DNA methyltransferases, histone deacetylases, and other corepressors, imposing a repressive chromatin state at differentiation-associated loci.

evidence.snippet: Here we found that conditional expression of promyelocytic leukemia-retinoic acid receptor alpha (PML-RARA), the protein encoded by the t(15;17) translocation found in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), suppressed PU.1 expression
evidence.explanation: Conditional PML-RARA expression suppresses a key myeloid-differentiation transcription factor.

steps/5.description: Repression of RARA-responsive and other myeloid genes prevents normal activation of the transcriptional program required for granulocyte maturation.

evidence.snippet: PMLRAR alpha transgenic mice exhibited impaired neutrophil maturation early in life, which progressed at a low frequency over the course of several months to overt APL.
evidence.explanation: The transgenic model connects impaired maturation to a preleukemic state and later APL.

steps/6.description: PML::RARA-expressing myeloid cells fail to complete neutrophil maturation, creating a preleukemic compartment from which overt APL can emerge.

evidence.snippet: Mechanistically, PML-RARa acts as a transcriptional repressor of RARa and non-RARa target genes and antagonizes the formation and function of PML nuclear bodies that regulate numerous signaling pathways.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports PML nuclear-body disruption by the fusion oncoprotein.

steps/7.description: PML::RARA disrupts the formation and signaling functions of PML nuclear bodies, compromising the tumor-suppressive programs coordinated by PML.

evidence.snippet: this simple (and sometimes sole) genetic alteration can transform hematopoietic progenitors through the acquisition of dominant-negative properties toward both transcriptional control by nuclear receptors and PML-mediated senescence
evidence.explanation: This supports failure of PML-mediated senescence in fusion-driven transformation.

steps/8.description: Dominant-negative impairment of PML-mediated senescence permits persistence and transformation of fusion-expressing hematopoietic progenitors.

evidence.snippet: Activating mutations in FLT3, including internal tandem duplication (ITD) in the juxtamembrane domain, transform hematopoietic cell lines to factor independent growth.
evidence.explanation: The model paper identifies the proliferative effect of activating FLT3-ITD.

steps/9.description: Activating FLT3 internal tandem duplication can provide a cooperating proliferative signal in PML::RARA-expressing hematopoietic cells. In the cited mouse model, the combination shortened leukemia latency and produced a fully penetrant APL-like disease; this node does not imply that FLT3-ITD is required in human APL.

evidence.snippet: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is characterized by proliferation of morphologically abnormal promyelocytes and a severe bleeding diathesis. The abnormal promyelocyte is characterized by abundant, large granules, many of which are spindle-shaped.
evidence.explanation: The overview describes the defining expansion and morphology of APL promyelocytes.

steps/10.description: Morphologically abnormal, granule-rich promyelocytes expand in bone marrow and can appear in peripheral blood.

evidence.snippet: The granules appear to possess tissue thromboplastin activity by both immunologic and clotting assays.
evidence.explanation: This is direct biochemical evidence of promyelocyte-associated procoagulant activity.

steps/11.description: Abnormal promyelocyte granules exhibit tissue thromboplastin activity, providing a direct route to systemic coagulation activation.

evidence.snippet: The differentiation of leukemic blasts and promyelocytes induced by ATRA and/or ATO may lead to cellular migration, endothelial activation, and release of interleukins and vascular factors responsible of tissue damage.
evidence.explanation: The review connects therapy-induced differentiation to the initiating events of differentiation syndrome.

steps/12.description: During induction, ATRA and/or ATO drive rapid differentiation of leukemic blasts and promyelocytes. This therapeutic response can also initiate the cellular migration and endothelial signaling that precede differentiation syndrome.

evidence.snippet: HP:0001876 | Pancytopenia | Frequent (79-30%)
evidence.explanation: Frequent pancytopenia supports impaired multilineage marrow output as a plausible intermediate.

steps/13.description: Expansion of the leukemic promyelocyte compartment is inferred to impair normal marrow output, providing a common intermediate for multilineage cytopenias. Available evidence here establishes the clinical associations, so these links remain partial rather than asserted as directly proven.

evidence.snippet: Coagulation studies in APL are generally consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation.
evidence.explanation: The source establishes the consumptive DIC pattern in APL.

evidence.snippet: However, there remains a considerable morbidity and mortality risk in APL secondary to clinically significant hemorrhagic and/or thrombotic events.
evidence.explanation: The updated review documents both hemorrhagic and thrombotic clinical consequences.

steps/14.description: APL produces a complex coagulopathy with clinically important hemorrhagic and thrombotic events. Consumptive coagulation is established, while modern reviews emphasize that the full hemostatic disturbance is broader than a single DIC mechanism.

evidence.snippet: The differentiation of leukemic blasts and promyelocytes induced by ATRA and/or ATO may lead to cellular migration, endothelial activation, and release of interleukins and vascular factors responsible of tissue damage.
evidence.explanation: The review supports a multi-component inflammatory and endothelial response rather than a cytokine-only model.

steps/15.description: Cellular migration, endothelial activation, interleukin and vascular-factor release, tissue infiltration, and capillary leak contribute to differentiation syndrome. The relative contribution of these mechanisms remains incompletely resolved.

evidence.snippet: Here we show in a child with microthrombocytopenia, eosinophilia and inflammatory disease, a homozygous frameshift mutation in ARPC1B (p.Val91Trpfs*30).
evidence.explanation: The founding observation and the first allele.

evidence.snippet: This would yield a product lacking five of the six WD40 repeat domains
evidence.explanation: Why this truncation is not a partial protein: it removes the beta-propeller surface that contacts the mother filament.

evidence.snippet: The disease-causing variants are diverse and scattered throughout the gene
evidence.explanation: Allelic heterogeneity across a 14-patient cohort, which is why no single variant defines the disease.

evidence.snippet: All cases harbored the founder splice-site variant c.64+2T>A in the ARPC1B gene.
evidence.explanation: The Nepalese founder allele.

steps/1.description:
Variants are diverse and scattered across the gene - frameshift, missense affecting the WD40 repeats, and splice-site - and in every patient tested the ARPC1B protein is undetectable on immunoblot. A splice-site founder variant, c.64+2T>A, accounts for a Nepalese cluster and is associated with a more severe course than other alleles.
The WD40 repeats matter structurally: six of them form the beta-propeller through which ARPC1B contacts the mother actin filament, so a truncation removing five of the six removes the interaction surface rather than merely shortening the protein.

evidence.snippet: Platelet lysates reveal no ARPC1B protein and greatly reduced Arp2/3 complex.
evidence.explanation: The complex-level consequence, measured directly in patient platelets.

evidence.snippet: Platelet levels of other Arp2/3 components (ARP2, ARP3, ARPC2, ARPC3 and ARPC5; Fig. 2b) and WASP (Fig. 2c) were normal in all patients
evidence.explanation: The other subunits are present. That is what makes this an assembly failure rather than a general loss of complex protein, and it also excludes a secondary WASP defect.

evidence.snippet: In agreement with recent experimental studies, our findings suggest that ARPC1 isoforms are not functionally interchangeable.
evidence.explanation: The conclusion this node is built on, and the reason ARPC1A upregulation is curated as a failed compensation rather than as a rescue.

evidence.snippet: In all patient samples tested, ARPC1B protein was undetectable by Western blotting and we identified an increased—although variable—expression of the ARPC1A isoform
evidence.explanation: Replication of both halves across 14 patients: no ARPC1B, more ARPC1A, disease anyway.

steps/2.description:
The rate-limiting node, and the one that makes this disease mechanistically interesting. ARPC1B-null platelets contain no ARPC1B and greatly reduced Arp2/3 complex, while the other five components are present at normal levels. So the complex is not merely missing a part; without this particular subunit it does not assemble.
ARPC1A is the obvious candidate substitute - same slot, 68% identity - and it is actively upregulated in ARPC1B-deficient cells. It does not rescue. Some ARPC1A does appear in the residual Arp2/3 of null platelets, where none is detectable in normal platelets, so the substitution physically happens and is simply not sufficient. The authors' conclusion, that the ARPC1 isoforms are not functionally interchangeable, is the human genetic evidence for a proposition that had only been argued experimentally.

evidence.snippet: defective platelet spreading with prominent filopodia but limited lammellipodia
evidence.explanation: The branched-versus-bundled morphological signature. Quoted with the source's own spelling of lamellipodia.

evidence.snippet: Human actin-related protein 2/3 complex (Arp2/3), required for actin filament branching, has two ARPC1 component isoforms, with ARPC1B prominently expressed in blood cells.
evidence.explanation: The complex's function and the expression pattern that confines the disease to haematopoietic lineages.

steps/3.description:
Arp2/3 nucleates a daughter filament off the side of an existing one, which is how cells build the branched networks that drive lamellipodia, phagocytosis, endocytosis, vesicular trafficking and immune-synapse formation. Losing it does not abolish actin polymerisation - patient platelets still spread, and still make prominent filopodia, which are unbranched bundles - it removes the branched arm specifically, leaving lamellipodia limited.
That morphological signature, filopodia preserved and lamellipodia lost, is the cellular fingerprint of the defect and is what connects the platelet, immune and DNA-repair arms below to one molecular lesion.

evidence.snippet: Knockout of ARPC1B in megakaryocytic cells results in decreased proplatelet formation, and as observed in platelets from patients, increased ARPC1A expression.
evidence.explanation: Locates the defect in the precursor. The same experiment also reproduces the ARPC1A upregulation seen in patients, which cross-validates the model.

steps/4.description: Knocking out ARPC1B in megakaryocytic cells decreases proplatelet formation, which puts the platelet defect upstream of the platelet: it is a production problem in the megakaryocyte, not only a functional problem in the circulating cell. Patient platelets additionally have dense granule deficiencies and the spreading abnormality above.

evidence.snippet: In vitro expanded Treg cells showed decreased expression of all Treg-cell markers including FOXP3, Helios, CD25, and CTLA-4
evidence.explanation: The Treg phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Impaired NK-cell degranulation in the presence of K562 cells was observed and similarly to patients6 with Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome IL-2 restored degranulation and killing to normal levels
evidence.explanation: The NK defect, its reversibility by IL-2, and the explicit parallel with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

evidence.snippet: In vitro T-cell proliferation in response to combination of anti-CD3+ 1 anti-CD28+, cytokines (IL-15, IL-2), and mitogens was largely normal
evidence.explanation: Rules out a general proliferation defect, which is what keeps this node about migration, synapse formation and degranulation.

steps/5.description:
The immune arm has been resolved to specific cell types. Regulatory T cells expanded from patients show decreased FOXP3, Helios, CD25 and CTLA-4 and defective suppressor activity against both CD4 and CD8 responders - a cell-intrinsic Treg defect, which is the most economical explanation for exaggerated Th2 responses, IgE reactivity and autoimmunity in one disease. NK cells show impaired degranulation against K562 targets, and, as in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, IL-2 restores it, which places the defect in signalling-dependent cytoskeletal remodelling rather than in the killing machinery.
Conventional T cells are reduced in number with a skewed naive compartment, but their proliferative responses are largely normal - so this is not a proliferation defect.

evidence.snippet: In particular, higher levels of chromatid-type aberrations and γH2AX foci, with an increased number of cells arrested in the G2/M-phase of the cell cycle, were found in patients' cells after ionizing radiation exposition and radiomimetic bleomycin treatment.
evidence.explanation: The three measurements behind the radiosensitivity claim.

evidence.snippet: ARPC1B is part of the actin-related protein 2/3 complex (Arp2/3) and cooperates with the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp) in the regulation of the actin cytoskeleton remodeling and in driving double-strand break clustering for homology-directed repair.
evidence.explanation: The proposed mechanism connecting the same complex to a nuclear function, which is why this arm hangs off the branched-nucleation node rather than off the immune one.

steps/6.description:
The newest and least-explored arm. Arp2/3 has a nuclear role: it promotes chromatin dynamics and drives clustering of DNA double-strand breaks for homology-directed repair. ARPC1B-deficient patient cells are radiosensitive by three independent methods, with more chromatid-type aberrations, more gamma-H2AX foci and more cells arrested in G2/M after ionising radiation or bleomycin.
This arm is curated separately rather than folded into the immune one because it is mechanistically distinct - it is nuclear, not cytoskeletal-motility - and because its clinical consequences are unknown. It was proposed as a disease trait in 2022 and has not been shown to cause any of the disease's manifestations.

evidence.snippet: Most patients (79%) (Fig 1, A) suffered from recurrent or severe bleeding episodes, most frequently represented by enterorrhagia.
evidence.explanation: Frequency and character of the bleeding, both of which this node depends on.

steps/7.description:
Bleeding is the presenting problem in most patients and is disproportionately gastrointestinal - enterorrhagia rather than the mucocutaneous bleeding a platelet count alone would predict. Nearly four in five patients in the largest cohort had recurrent or severe bleeding.
Whether these platelets are small is disputed, and the dispute is not cosmetic: platelet size is the classical bedside discriminator against Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. See the controversy discussion below.

evidence.snippet: The disease is characterized by a very early clinical onset (mean, 2 months; range, 1–6 months)
evidence.explanation: Age of onset.

evidence.snippet: Cutaneous vasculitis was noted in 69% of patients, presenting as a maculopapular rash, erythema nodosum, or vasculitic purpura

evidence.snippet: In contrast to Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome or DOCK8 deficiency,5 the humoral response to polysaccharide vaccine was normal in most cases

steps/8.description: Very early onset - a mean of two months, with a range of one to six - and a triad that would ordinarily suggest three diagnoses: susceptibility to infection, allergy, and autoimmune inflammation. Recurrent or severe respiratory infection in 71% and skin infection in 50%; eczema in 57% with food allergy and asthma; cutaneous vasculitis in 69%, leukocytoclastic on every biopsy performed; arthritis in 23%. IgA and IgE are markedly raised in almost all cases, while the antibody response to polysaccharide vaccine is normal - unlike Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome or DOCK8 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: A next-generation sequencing (NGS) gene panel analysis focused on 407 genes related to IEIs showed a previously unreported homozygous intronic deletion on ARPC1B gene (c.64 + 4_64 + 24DEL). genes/0.notes:
Variants are scattered through the gene and span four consequence classes: frameshift (p.Val91Trpfs*30), missense affecting the WD40 repeats (p.Ala105Val, p.Ala238Thr), splice site (the Nepalese founder allele c.64+2T>A), and - importantly for how the gene is tested - two lesions that a coding-consequence filter would not flag at all: the synonymous c.783G>A (p.Ala261Ala), which disrupts splicing, and the intronic c.64+4_64+24del.
The founder allele c.64+2T>A is associated with a more severe phenotype and worse long-term outcome than other variants. Expressivity is otherwise wide even within a family: the three siblings homozygous for c.783G>A were reported for the significant intrafamilial clinical heterogeneity of their presentation, and that same genotype produces the syndrome without thrombocytopenia.

evidence.snippet: The absence of a direct effect on actin cytoskeleton may also explain the lack of efficacy of sirolimus in previously reported ARPC1B-deficient patients affected by broader immune dysregulation features, including at least three or more systems involved.

treatments/4.description:
An mTOR inhibitor, reported to control refractory relapsing thrombocytopenia in a patient with an isolated-cytopenia phenotype, along with the lymphoproliferation and autoantibodies.
The mechanistic finding is the interesting part and it constrains the indication. Actin polymerisation assays before and after treatment showed no significant difference, so sirolimus is not correcting the Arp2/3 defect - the authors read the benefit as immunomodulatory, reducing autoimmunity. That is also offered as the explanation for why sirolimus failed in previously reported patients with broader immune dysregulation. So this is a treatment for the autoimmune component in a mild phenotype, not a treatment for ARPC1B deficiency, and an entry that recorded it without the assay result would imply the latter.

treatments/5.description: Intravenous immunoglobulin was used in the reported sirolimus case, initially for immune thrombocytopenia at 2 g/kg and subsequently as maintenance. Curated at that strength: a single documented case course, not a cohort practice.

evidence.snippet: In particular, higher levels of chromatid-type aberrations and γH2AX foci, with an increased number of cells arrested in the G2/M-phase of the cell cycle, were found in patients' cells after ionizing radiation exposition and radiomimetic bleomycin treatment.

treatments/6.description:
A precaution rather than a therapy, and the actionable half of the radiosensitivity finding. Patient cells show increased chromatid aberrations, gamma-H2AX foci and G2/M arrest after ionising radiation *and* after bleomycin, so the exposure to avoid is not only radiotherapy.
Two contexts make this concrete: transplantation is the only curative option and conditioning intensity is chosen partly on DNA-repair status, and bleomycin is a conventional chemotherapy agent. The clinical consequences are unestablished - that remains an open knowledge gap - but the authors themselves call for the trait to be investigated in order to optimise therapeutic interventions, and a precaution costs nothing while the question is open.

open_questions/0.rationale:
Three sources, two answers. The founding report describes microthrombocytopenia in its index child and states that patient platelets are microthrombocytes similar to those seen in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome - that resemblance is part of why ARPC1B was pursued as a WAS-like candidate gene at all. The 14-patient cohort reports reduced platelet counts with normal volume in most cases. The IUIS 2022 classification table records mild thrombocytopenia with normal-sized platelets, siding with the cohort.
This is not a detail. Platelet size is the classical bedside discriminator between Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and its mimics, and it is one of the three separators this entry's differential-diagnosis section relies on. If normal-sized platelets do not exclude ARPC1B deficiency, then a WAS-like child with normal platelet volume still needs the gene tested.
An allelic reconciliation is the obvious first guess - the founding cases include a complete-null frameshift and a near-null missense pair, while the cohort spans variants scattered across the gene - and the founding paper's own discussion argues against it. Microthrombocytes were seen in all three of its patients, spanning both allele classes, while platelet *counts* varied between them: always low in the frameshift patient, low to normal in one missense sibling and normal in the other. So in that series genotype tracked count and not size, which is the opposite of what the allelic hypothesis needs.
That leaves measurement as the more likely explanation - platelet sizing is method-dependent, and small platelets are easy to lose at the lower gate of an automated analyser - but no cited source compares methods, so this stays a controversy rather than a resolution.
One later report widens the question from size to presence. Three siblings homozygous for the synonymous c.783G>A allele have the syndrome with **no thrombocytopenia at all**. That does not settle the size disagreement, but it does mean the platelet phenotype in ARPC1B deficiency is not a fixed feature to be characterised so much as a variable one to be stratified - and it is a further reason not to use platelet findings to include or exclude the diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: Growth failure was noted in all patients (Table E2), with growth hormone tests found to be impaired when performed (P2 and P3), compatible with a partial growth hormone deficiency, and no catch-up growth after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) (P2, P3, and P6).
evidence.explanation: All three components of the argument in one sentence: universality, the pituitary lead, and the failure of transplant to correct it.

open_questions/1.rationale:
Growth failure is universal in the largest cohort, growth hormone testing was impaired where it was performed, and there was no catch-up growth after transplantation in the three patients where it could be assessed. Transplantation otherwise works: it resolves the autoinflammatory features and leaves patients off medication.
The dissociation is informative about where the disease acts. If growth failure were secondary to chronic inflammation and recurrent infection, correcting those should permit catch-up. It did not. Two readings remain, and the cited literature does not choose between them: either the growth deficit is established irreversibly before transplant, or it has a non-haematopoietic component - which would be surprising for a gene whose expression is described as predominantly haematopoietic, and would be the more interesting answer.
The partial growth hormone deficiency is the concrete lead. It was found in two patients and points at the pituitary, which is not a haematopoietic tissue and would not be replaced by a transplant.

evidence.snippet: Overall, our data suggest increased radiosensitivity as an additional trait in ARPC1B deficiency and support the necessity to investigate this feature in ARPC1B patients as well as in other IEI with cytoskeleton defects to address specific clinical follow-up and optimize therapeutic interventions.
evidence.explanation: Curated as PARTIAL because the authors' own framing is a suggestion plus a call for investigation - the clinical consequence is exactly what has not been established.

open_questions/2.rationale:
Radiosensitivity was proposed as a disease trait in 2022 on the basis of three assays in a small number of patients. Nothing links it to any clinical event. That matters specifically because transplantation is the only curative treatment for this disease and conditioning regimens are chosen partly on DNA-repair status - a radiosensitive patient conditioned as though they were not is a real hazard, and the authors say as much when they call for this to be investigated to optimise therapeutic interventions.
The gap is that nobody has looked at outcomes. The transplanted patients reported in the literature were not, so far as the cited sources record, stratified by radiosensitivity, and none of the sources read for this entry reports a malignancy outcome in an ARPC1B-deficient patient - the malignancy discussion in the founding paper is about Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and about ARPC1 isoforms in sporadic tumours, not about these patients.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report that enduring AZT treatment of T-cell leukemia virus I-infected cells, in vitro and in vivo in ATL patients, results in inhibition of telomerase activity, progressive telomere shortening, and increased p14(ARF) expression. In turn, this elicits stabilization and reactivation of the tumor suppressor p53-dependent transcription, increased expression of the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21(Waf1), and accumulation of p27(kip1), thereby inducing cellular senescence and tumor cell death.

evidence.snippet: In the entire cohort, median survival of patients with and without TP53 mutations was 1·0 and 6·7 years respectively (P < 0·001).

The modeled mechanism is explicitly bounded to this treatment context.

evidence.snippet: Heterozygous inversions in chromosome 15q21.2-3, which caused the coding region of the aromatase gene to lie adjacent to constitutively active cryptic promoters that normally transcribe other genes, resulted in severe estrogen excess owing to the overexpression of aromatase in many tissues.
evidence.explanation: The original AEXS gain-of-function report establishes the promoter-swap mechanism driving aromatase overexpression.

evidence.snippet: Duplications appear to have caused CYP19A1 overexpression because of an increased number of physiological promoters, whereas deletions and inversions would have induced wide CYP19A1 expression due to the formation of chimeric genes consisting of a noncoding exon(s) of a neighboring gene and CYP19A1 coding exons.
evidence.explanation: Distinguishes the duplication (extra native promoters) from the deletion/inversion (chimeric ectopic promoter) routes to overexpression.

evidence.snippet: We identified three types of heterozygous genomic rearrangements, i.e. a 79,156-bp tandem duplication involving seven of 11 noncoding CYP19A1 exons 1, a 211,631-bp deletion involving exons 2-43 of DMXL2 and exons 5-10 of GLDN, and a 165,901-bp deletion involving exons 2-43 of DMXL2.
evidence.explanation: Reports the specific heterozygous duplications and deletions underlying AEXS.

steps/1.description: Heterozygous submicroscopic rearrangements at chromosome 15q21.2 drive CYP19A1 overexpression by two routes: tandem duplications increase the copy number of the native tissue-specific promoters, while deletions and inversions juxtapose the CYP19A1 coding region with constitutively active or ectopic promoters of neighboring genes (e.g., TMOD3, DMXL2, GLDN, CGNL1, MAPK6, TLN2), forming chimeric transcripts. The aromatase protein itself is structurally normal; its expression is pathologically increased and broadened across tissues.

evidence.snippet: Markedly increased aromatase activity was found in the patients' fibroblasts and Epstein-Barr virus-transformed lymphocytes.
evidence.explanation: Directly measures markedly increased aromatase activity in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: Aromatase activity and mRNA levels in fat and skin and whole-body aromatization of androstenedione were severely elevated.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies severely elevated aromatase activity and whole-body aromatization.

steps/2.description: Aromatase overexpression raises total and extraglandular aromatase activity; whole-body aromatization of androgens is markedly elevated. The enzyme is catalytically normal, so the change is quantitative (more activity), not a novel catalytic function.

evidence.snippet: hCG testing demonstrated a high rate of conversion of delta4-androstenedione to estrone and of testosterone to estradiol in the propositus and his father.

steps/3.description: Excess aromatization raises circulating estradiol and estrone and the estrogen-to-androgen ratio. Estrogen negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis suppresses gonadotropins, and downstream estrogen action drives the skeletal and breast phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: Gynecomastia of prepubertal onset may result from increased estrogen owing to excessive aromatase activity in extraglandular tissues.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous gain-of-function structural rearrangements at 15q21.2 fall into three variant classes: tandem duplications (which raise CYP19A1 dosage via extra native promoters) and deletions and inversions (which recruit novel ectopic promoters of neighboring genes to form chimeric CYP19A1 transcripts). No CYP19A1 coding-sequence point mutations cause AEXS; loss-of-function CYP19A1 point mutations instead cause the opposite disease, aromatase deficiency. Phenotypic severity is not uniform across the classes: it is determined by the tissue-expression pattern of the driving promoter and the structural property of the fused promoter-associated exons (in particular whether the chimeric first exon carries a natural translation start codon).

evidence.snippet: We narrowed the candidate region and have identified a new gene encoding a member of the histidine triad (HIT) superfamily as the 'causative' gene. We have called its product aprataxin; the gene symbol is APTX.
evidence.explanation: The gene identification, from one of the two 2001 papers that reported it independently.

evidence.snippet: Aprataxin is a member of the histidine triad (HIT) family of nucleotide hydrolases and transferases, and inactivating mutations are largely confined to this HIT domain.
evidence.explanation: Localises the disease-causing mutations to the catalytic domain, which is what makes the enzymatic model of this disease a mechanism rather than a correlation.

evidence.snippet: Expression of mutated proteins in lymphocytes from these patients was greatly decreased.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived confirmation that these alleles reduce protein, not only activity.

steps/1.description:
Aprataxin is built from three modules - an N-terminal region homologous to polynucleotide kinase phosphatase, a histidine-triad (HIT) nucleotide-hydrolase domain, and a C2H2 zinc finger. Inactivating mutations are largely confined to the HIT domain, which is the catalytic one, and patient lymphocytes show greatly decreased protein.
The recurrent alleles are population-specific (W279X, W279R and P206L recur across European series), which is why AOA1 is the commonest recessive ataxia in Japan and second only to Friedreich ataxia in Portugal while accounting for around 5-6% of non-Friedreich recessive ataxia in mixed European cohorts.

evidence.snippet: Specifically, aprataxin catalyses the nucleophilic release of adenylate groups covalently linked to 5'-phosphate termini at single-strand nicks and gaps, resulting in the production of 5'-phosphate termini that can be efficiently rejoined.
evidence.explanation: The enzymatic reaction this node is built on, stated at chemical resolution.

evidence.snippet: Aprataxin associates with the DNA repair proteins XRCC1 and XRCC4, which are partners of DNA ligase III and ligase IV, respectively, suggestive of a role in DNA repair.
evidence.explanation: Places aprataxin physically at both the single-strand-break and double-strand-break ligase complexes, which is how it reaches its substrate.

steps/2.description:
The rate-limiting lesion, and the reason this disease is mechanistically specific rather than a generic repair failure. DNA ligase works through an adenylated intermediate; when the reaction aborts, the adenylate is left covalently attached to the 5'-phosphate of the nick. That terminus is now chemically blocked - ligase cannot re-attack it, so the break is not merely unrepaired but unrepairable by the pathway that created it.
Aprataxin's contribution is to release the adenylate and restore a 5'-phosphate that ligase can use. So the enzyme does not repair DNA; it repairs the repair machinery's own mistakes. That distinction matters for the disease, because it predicts damage proportional to ligation activity rather than to exogenous genotoxic exposure - which is consistent with a phenotype restricted to long-lived post-mitotic neurons and with the absence of the organism-level radiosensitivity seen in ataxia-telangiectasia.

evidence.snippet: Consistent with this, APTX-defective cell lines are sensitive to agents that cause single-strand breaks and exhibit an increased incidence of induced chromosomal aberrations.
evidence.explanation: The cellular repair deficit, measured.

evidence.snippet: These data indicate that neurological disorders associated with APTX mutations may be caused by the gradual accumulation of unrepaired DNA strand breaks resulting from abortive DNA ligation events.
evidence.explanation: Curated as PARTIAL rather than SUPPORT because the authors write "may be caused by". The biochemistry is demonstrated; the link to neurodegeneration is proposed.

steps/3.description: Aprataxin-defective cells are hypersensitive to single-strand-break-inducing agents and show more induced chromosomal aberrations, so the repair deficit is demonstrable in the laboratory. The proposal that the neurological disease arises from gradual accumulation of these breaks is the authors' own inference from that biochemistry, and is curated here as the mechanism it is - a model that explains the cell-type selectivity of a ubiquitously expressed protein, not a lesion measured in patient brain.

evidence.snippet: Cerebellar ataxia with cerebellar atrophy on MRI and severe axonal sensorimotor neuropathy were present in all patients.
evidence.explanation: Cerebellar atrophy in 14 of 14 mutation-positive patients. The same sentence carries the neuropathy arm.

evidence.snippet: It shares several neurological features with ataxia-telangiectasia, including early onset ataxia, oculomotor apraxia and cerebellar atrophy, but does not share its extraneurological features (immune deficiency, chromosomal instability and hypersensitivity to X-rays).
evidence.explanation: The comparison that defines the entity's boundary: the same neurological syndrome as ataxia-telangiectasia without any of its systemic features.

steps/4.description:
Cerebellar atrophy on MRI is present in every reported patient, alongside the ataxia. The module this node conforms to explicitly admits a DNA-repair insult as one of the heterogeneous triggers converging on cerebellar neuron stress, which is exactly the entry point AOA1 uses.
Conformance stops at the insult node deliberately. The module's downstream Purkinje Neuron Degeneration node is a cellular claim, and no neuropathological study of AOA1 was found among the references read for this entry; MRI atrophy is a tissue-level observation and does not establish which cerebellar neuron is lost.

evidence.snippet: Cerebellar ataxia with cerebellar atrophy on MRI and severe axonal sensorimotor neuropathy were present in all patients.
evidence.explanation: Universal severe axonal sensorimotor neuropathy in the cohort.

evidence.snippet: AOA1 is also characterized by axonal motor neuropathy and the later decrease of serum albumin levels and elevation of total cholesterol.
evidence.explanation: Axonal character of the neuropathy, and the late timing of the biochemical markers.

steps/5.description: A severe axonal sensorimotor neuropathy is present in every reported patient and becomes the dominant feature in young adults, at which point it can partially mask the cerebellar signs. AOA1 is a predominantly axonal neuropathy, which the module's central effector node explicitly covers alongside the demyelinating route.

evidence.snippet: The mean age at onset was 6.8 +/- 4.8 years (range 2-18 years).
evidence.explanation: Age of onset in the mutation-confirmed cohort.

evidence.snippet: Ocular saccade initiation was normal, but their duration was increased by the succession of multiple hypometric saccades that could clinically be confused with 'slow saccades'.
evidence.explanation: The oculographic correction this node's description is written around.

steps/6.description:
Onset is in childhood, with a mean around seven years. Oculomotor apraxia is the eponymous sign but is not universal and is most prominent early.
One measurement in the Le Ber series is worth carrying because it corrects a common bedside impression: saccade initiation is actually normal in AOA1. What looks like slow saccades is a train of multiple hypometric saccades taking longer to reach target. A clinician recording "slow saccades" would be describing the right abnormality with the wrong mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Cerebellar ataxia and/or chorea predominate at onset, but later on they are often partially masked by severe neuropathy, which is the most typical symptom in young adults.
evidence.explanation: The temporal inversion, stated directly by the source.

evidence.snippet: hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia, and cognitive impairment are present in the adult stage
evidence.explanation: Independent statement that the biochemical markers and the cognitive phenotype belong to the adult stage rather than to presentation.

steps/7.description: The inversion of the syndrome over time. Cerebellar ataxia and chorea lead at onset; in young adults the neuropathy is the most typical symptom and partially masks them. A patient first seen in adulthood may therefore present as a neuropathy rather than as an ataxia, which is a real diagnostic trap for an ataxia gene panel ordered on phenotype.

genes/0.notes: Recurrent alleles include W279X, W279R, A198V, D267G and P206L. Mutations are largely confined to the HIT domain.

evidence.snippet: Treatment of manifestations: May include physical therapy, particularly for disabilities resulting from peripheral neuropathy; a wheelchair for mobility, usually by age 15-20 years; educational support for difficulties with speaking, reading, and writing.
evidence.explanation: The published management recommendations are entirely supportive. That is the evidence for this node's claim: what is recommended is what you recommend when there is nothing disease-modifying to give.

treatments/0.description:
There is no disease-modifying therapy. Nothing in the literature read for this entry modifies the aprataxin defect or the accumulation of unrepaired strand breaks, and this entry states that as a finding rather than leaving it to be inferred from an empty section. Everything below is supportive, and the published management recommendations are functional and preventive rather than mechanistic.
Coenzyme Q10 has been discussed as an investigational option on the assumption of a secondary coenzyme Q10 deficiency. The one series in this entry's reference set that measured it found normal levels in five of six patients, which is why it is not curated as a treatment - see the interpretation discussion.

evidence.snippet: Treatment of manifestations: May include physical therapy, particularly for disabilities resulting from peripheral neuropathy; a wheelchair for mobility, usually by age 15-20 years; educational support for difficulties with speaking, reading, and writing.
evidence.explanation: The recommendation and the age at which mobility support is typically needed.

treatments/1.description: Directed at the neuropathy rather than at the ataxia, which matches where the disability comes from: a wheelchair is usually needed by fifteen to twenty years of age.

evidence.snippet: Treatment of manifestations: May include physical therapy, particularly for disabilities resulting from peripheral neuropathy; a wheelchair for mobility, usually by age 15-20 years; educational support for difficulties with speaking, reading, and writing.

evidence.snippet: Prevention of secondary complications: High-protein diet to prevent edema by restoring serum albumin concentration; low-cholesterol diet.
evidence.explanation: Both dietary recommendations and the stated purpose of the first, which is what the mechanistic assumption above is read from.

treatments/2.description:
Aimed at the two biochemical markers rather than at the neurological disease: a high-protein diet to prevent oedema by restoring serum albumin, and a low-cholesterol diet for the hypercholesterolaemia.
This is more interesting than a supportive measure usually is, because it embeds a mechanistic assumption. Recommending protein intake to raise albumin presumes the hypoalbuminaemia is substrate-limited - a synthesis or intake problem - rather than a catabolic one. Nothing in the literature read here tests that presumption, and the knowledge-gap discussion is written around it.

evidence.snippet: Surveillance: Routine follow up with a neurologist.
evidence.explanation: The recommended surveillance.

evidence.snippet: Carrier testing for at-risk family members and prenatal testing for pregnancies at increased risk are possible if both pathogenic variants in a family have been identified.
evidence.explanation: The availability and its precondition.

treatments/4.description: Available once both pathogenic variants in the family are identified, and worth offering because the recurrence risk in siblings is the standard recessive 25%.

evidence.snippet: Treatment of manifestations: May include physical therapy, particularly for disabilities resulting from peripheral neuropathy; a wheelchair for mobility, usually by age 15-20 years; educational support for difficulties with speaking, reading, and writing.
evidence.explanation: Educational support as a named management recommendation.

treatments/5.description: Named in the management recommendations alongside physical therapy, and directed at difficulties with speaking, reading and writing - which matters given that cognitive involvement is common and dysarthria is an early feature.

evidence.snippet: AOA1 is also characterized by axonal motor neuropathy and the later decrease of serum albumin levels and elevation of total cholesterol.
evidence.explanation: The association and its late timing, stated without any mechanism - which is the gap itself.

evidence.snippet: Prevention of secondary complications: High-protein diet to prevent edema by restoring serum albumin concentration; low-cholesterol diet.
evidence.explanation: The management recommendation whose rationale presumes a substrate-limited mechanism. Curated as INDIRECT: it is evidence about what is believed and recommended, not evidence that the belief is correct.

open_questions/0.rationale:
Hypoalbuminaemia is written into the disease's own MONDO and OMIM labels, yet none of the references read for this entry offers a mechanism. Every source treats it as an association: the 2001 gene papers report it as a clinical characteristic, the 2003 French series and the 2011 Italian series quantify it, and the 2008 report places it in the adult stage. The searches run for this entry found nothing addressing the causal step, so the pathograph deliberately does not connect it to the APTX lesion by an edge.
The gap is worth stating rather than papering over, because dismech now also holds an entry in which hypoalbuminaemia *is* mechanistically explained - hypercatabolic hypoproteinaemia, where FcRn salvage failure raises the catabolic rate of albumin. A protein-turnover study in AOA1 of the kind Waldmann and Terry performed in 1968 would settle in one experiment whether the albumin here is under-synthesised or over-catabolised, and nothing in the literature curated here reports one.
Management practice has quietly taken a side. The published recommendation is a high-protein diet to prevent oedema by restoring serum albumin - which only makes sense if the albumin is substrate-limited, that is, a synthesis or intake problem. If AOA1 hypoalbuminaemia were catabolic in the way hypercatabolic hypoproteinaemia's is, eating more protein would raise the flux through a leak rather than fix it, and the FcRn disease is the demonstration: those patients synthesise albumin at a normal rate and are still hypoalbuminaemic.
So the assumption is testable and, so far as the literature read here goes, untested. It is also not idle: it is the stated rationale of a dietary recommendation given to patients.

evidence.snippet: However, a remarkably severe and persistent choreic phenotype was associated with one of the mutations (A198V).
evidence.explanation: The allele-specific claim.

evidence.snippet: The clinical phenotype was homogeneous, irrespectively of the type and location of the APTX mutation
evidence.explanation: The opposing claim. Curated as REFUTE of the general genotype-phenotype proposition, not as a refutation of the A198V observation specifically, which this cohort had no opportunity to test.

open_questions/1.rationale:
Two large series disagree. The 2003 French series singles out A198V as producing a remarkably severe and persistent chorea, against the usual pattern in which chorea fades. The 2011 Italian series states flatly that the phenotype was homogeneous irrespective of mutation type and location.
The disagreement may be smaller than it looks: A198V does not appear among the alleles reported in the Italian cohort, which found W279X, W279R and P206L homozygotes plus three novel truncating variants. A series that never observed the allele cannot contradict a claim about it. Recorded as a controversy rather than resolved in either direction, because settling it needs a cohort carrying A198V and scored for chorea persistence, which neither series is.

evidence.snippet: Analyses of coenzyme Q10 in muscle, fibroblasts, and plasma demonstrated normal levels of coenzyme in five of six mutated subjects.
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement against the secondary-coenzyme-Q10-deficiency proposal, in three tissues.

open_questions/2.rationale:
AOA1 has been discussed alongside the secondary coenzyme Q10 deficiencies, which would give it a mitochondrial arm and a supplement with a rationale. The one series in this entry's reference set that actually measured it found normal coenzyme Q10 in muscle, fibroblasts and plasma in five of six mutation-positive subjects.
That is a small number and a negative result, so it does not close the question. It is enough, though, to keep a mitochondrial node out of this pathograph: there is no measured coenzyme Q10 deficit to build one on, and inventing the node would create a therapeutic rationale the data do not support.

evidence.snippet: Cognitive impairment was always present.
evidence.explanation: The universality claim.

evidence.snippet: Intellect remains normal in some individuals; in others, different degrees of cognitive impairment have been observed.
evidence.explanation: The opposing claim, from the disease's GeneReviews chapter.

open_questions/3.rationale:
Two sources make incompatible universal claims. The 14-patient French series states that cognitive impairment was always present. The GeneReviews chapter states that intellect remains normal in some individuals, with varying degrees of impairment in others.
Both cannot be right as stated, and the disagreement is not resolvable from the abstracts curated here because neither reports the instrument used. "Cognitive impairment" assessed by formal neuropsychological battery and "intellect remains normal" assessed clinically can coexist in the same population: a patient with normal measured IQ and impaired executive or processing-speed performance would be counted in both categories by the two sources. Cerebellar cognitive-affective changes are exactly the kind that a global intellect judgement misses.
The phenotype band was lowered from OBLIGATE to FREQUENT rather than picking a winner, because a band should not assert more than the weaker of two conflicting sources allows.
A caveat on weighting: the GeneReviews chapter is formally retired and its own header warns the information may be out of date, so it is not automatically the better source. It is, however, the only one of the two that reports the observation prospectively across the disease's described natural history rather than in one ascertained cohort.

evidence.snippet: The first manifestation is progressive gait imbalance (mean age of onset: 4.3 years; range: 2-10 years), followed by dysarthria, then upper-limb dysmetria with mild intention tremor.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews onset figures.

evidence.snippet: The mean age at onset was 6.8 +/- 4.8 years (range 2-18 years).
evidence.explanation: The cohort figure. Curated as PARTIAL of the onset claim because it is a referral-series denominator, which is the point of this discussion.

open_questions/4.rationale:
The GeneReviews chapter gives a mean onset of 4.3 years with a range of 2 to 10. The French series gives 6.8 plus or minus 4.8 years with a range of 2 to 18. The lower bound agrees; the upper bound differs by eight years.
The likely explanation is ascertainment rather than disagreement. The French figure comes from screening a referred series of 158 non-Friedreich recessive ataxia families, which will include patients who presented late enough to be mistaken for something else; the GeneReviews figure describes the disease as characterised in dedicated AOA1 series. A referral-based denominator shifts a mean onset upward and widens the range in exactly this way.
Both are recorded rather than averaged. For counselling, the wider range is the safer one: a first presentation at fifteen does not exclude AOA1.

evidence.explanation: Segregation of a T-box-domain TBX20 variant with congenital heart disease across three generations.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, Tbx20-I121M resulted in a significantly enhanced transcriptional activity, which was further increased in the presence of co-transcription factors GATA4/5 and NKX2-5.
evidence.explanation: Sources the gain-of-function half of the mechanism recorded in these notes, and the interaction with the other septation transcription factors curated in this entry.

evidence.snippet: Our data, combined with that of others, suggest that human ASDII may be related to loss-of-function as well as gain-of-function TBX20 mutations.
evidence.explanation: Sources the claim in these notes that both directions of effect have been reported, which is why the mechanism is not simple haploinsufficiency.

genes/4.notes: TBX20 is the gene of atrial septal defect 4 (MONDO:0012654, OMIM 611363). Both loss-of-function and gain-of-function T-box-domain variants have been reported, so the mechanism is not a simple haploinsufficiency. ClinGen's Congenital Heart Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel grades TBX20 against the broader concept congenital heart disease (MONDO:0005453, autosomal dominant, SOP10) as Moderate, in assertion CGGV:assertion_67706e90-ac03-4b96-94e2-4a561ced4a41-2024-05-07T050000.000Z classified 2024-05-07; read from the ClinGen Gene-Disease Validity CSV snapshot committed in this repository (file creation date 2026-01-24). No ClinGen assertion exists against an atrial-septal-defect term.

evidence.snippet: A mutation screen of the coding regions of ACTC1 revealed a founder mutation predicting an M123V substitution in affected individuals of both pedigrees.
evidence.explanation: The founder variant segregating with isolated dominant secundum ASD in two pedigrees.

evidence.snippet: Morpholino (MO) knockdown of ACTC1 in chick embryos produces delayed looping and reduced atrial septa, supporting a developmental role for this protein.
evidence.explanation: Developmental perturbation evidence linking reduced ACTC1 to deficient atrial septum formation.

evidence.snippet: Functional analysis of ACTC1 with an M123V substitution shows a reduced affinity for myosin, but with retained actomyosin motor properties.
evidence.explanation: Sources the myosin-affinity claim recorded in these notes.

genes/5.notes: ACTC1 encodes alpha-cardiac actin and is the gene of atrial septal defect 5 (MONDO:0013011, OMIM 612794). It is one of the two sarcomeric members of the numbered ASD series, alongside MYH6 in ASD3; the reported founder M123V substitution reduces affinity for myosin while retaining actomyosin motor function. ClinGen has curated ACTC1 three times, against hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Definitive), dilated cardiomyopathy (Moderate) and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (No Known Disease Relationship), but against no atrial-septal-defect or congenital-heart-disease term, in the ClinGen Gene-Disease Validity CSV snapshot committed in this repository (file creation date 2026-01-24).

evidence.snippet: In four nonrelated patients, three missense mutations in coding sequence, and one single base change in the 5'UTR have been detected.
evidence.explanation: The entirety of the human genetic evidence in the defining report, which is the basis for the UNKNOWN typing here.

evidence.snippet: Incomplete heart septation similar to ASD was reported in transgenic mice with both inactive alleles of gene encoding mammalian zinc metalloprotease a mammalian tolloid-like 1 (tll1).
evidence.explanation: The mouse null phenotype that motivated the human screen, quoted from this report's own introduction rather than from its results.

genes/6.notes: TLL1 encodes the zinc metalloprotease tolloid-like 1 and is the gene of atrial septal defect 6 (MONDO:0013123, OMIM 613087). The human evidence is three missense changes and one 5'UTR change across four unrelated patients in a 19-patient screen, with no segregation data; the mouse null shows incomplete septation. ClinGen's Congenital Heart Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel grades TLL1 against congenital heart disease (MONDO:0005453, autosomal dominant, SOP10) as Limited, in assertion CGGV:assertion_37ed8aea-d2e0-4bab-9e21-4f5ac823ce99-2024-05-13T160000.000Z classified 2024-05-13; read from the ClinGen Gene-Disease Validity CSV snapshot committed in this repository (file creation date 2026-01-24). Limited means insufficient evidence rather than refutation, so this record is typed UNKNOWN and is deliberately not bound to a pathophysiology node.

evidence.snippet: In summary, the observation of these mutations in patients with septal defects indicates that CITED2 has a causative impact in the development of CHD in humans.
evidence.explanation: The defining report's conclusion for the septal-defect phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Here we show that these mutations significantly reduce the capacity of CITED2 to transrepress HIF1A, and that the p.Ser170_Gly178del mutation significantly diminishes TFAP2C coactivation.
evidence.explanation: Functional consequence of the reported variants, and the source of the HIF1A and TFAP2 detail in these notes.

evidence.snippet: All three of these amino acid changing mutations cluster in the serine-glycine-rich junction of the protein, to which no functionality had heretofore been assigned.
evidence.explanation: Sources the claim in these notes that the reported variants cluster in a previously unassigned region.

genes/7.notes: CITED2 is the gene of atrial septal defect 8 (MONDO:0013750, OMIM 614433). It encodes a CREBBP/EP300-interacting transcriptional modulator of HIF1A and TFAP2, and the reported variants cluster in a serine-glycine-rich junction whose function was previously unassigned. ClinGen's Congenital Heart Disease Gene Curation Expert Panel grades CITED2 against congenital heart disease (MONDO:0005453, autosomal dominant, SOP9) as Moderate, in assertion CGGV:assertion_007f4832-e639-4b27-9cc0-8b8cfaf45534-2023-09-05T160000.000Z classified 2023-09-05; read from the ClinGen Gene-Disease Validity CSV snapshot committed in this repository (file creation date 2026-01-24). No ClinGen assertion exists against an atrial-septal-defect term.

evidence.snippet: The same heterozygous missense mutation (Ser184Asn) was identified in three patients, including one with tetralogy of Fallot and two with atrial septal defects.
evidence.explanation: Two of the three variant carriers in this sporadic congenital heart defect cohort had atrial septal defects.

evidence.snippet: Biological analysis revealed clearly decreased transcriptional activity of GATA6 Ser184Asn in vitro.
evidence.explanation: Functional support for reduced GATA6 transcriptional activity as the mechanism of the reported variant.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in GATA4 have been related to human congenital heart diseases (CHDs) in several studies, whereas mutations in GATA6 have only recently been reported in patients with persistent truncus arteriosus.
evidence.explanation: Sources the outflow-tract origin of the human GATA6 phenotype recorded in these notes, quoted from this report's own background.

genes/8.notes: GATA6 is the gene of atrial septal defect 9 (MONDO:0013770, OMIM 614475). MONDO carries no causal-gene edge on that term; the assignment comes from its OMIM and MedGen 482573 record, whose cytogenetic location 18q11.2 matches GATA6 in HGNC. The first reported human GATA6 variants were in persistent truncus arteriosus, an outflow-tract malformation, and the broader GATA6 claim including pancreatic and endocrine disease is curated in Congenital_Heart_Disease and Pancreatic_Agenesis; ClinGen grades GATA6-related congenital heart disease with or without pancreatic agenesis or neonatal diabetes (MONDO:0100540, autosomal dominant) as Definitive, in assertion CGGV:assertion_a7a0fdd7-f796-4921-95b6-709fd859b6d3-2023-11-21T170000.000Z classified 2023-11-21; read from the ClinGen Gene-Disease Validity CSV snapshot committed in this repository (file creation date 2026-01-24). This record carries only the atrial-septal presentation.

treatments/1.description: Device closure is generally preferred for hemodynamically significant secundum ASD when defect size, rims, and pulmonary vascular status are suitable. Severe irreversible pulmonary vascular disease or Eisenmenger physiology is a contraindication; uncertain pulmonary vascular or left ventricular physiology requires specialist invasive assessment before closure.

evidence.snippet: ASDII results in right-sided volume unloading

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Device occlusion terminates the atrial-level shunt and unloads the right heart when closure is physiologically appropriate.

evidence.snippet: Transcatheter and surgical techniques both provide valid options for ASDII closure, the former being the preferred method.
evidence.explanation: The review supports surgery as a valid ASDII closure option, while noting that transcatheter closure is preferred when suitable.

evidence.snippet: With the exception of those with severe and irreversible PAH, closure is beneficial to, and thus indicated in all patients with significant shunts, regardless of age and symptoms.
evidence.explanation: This supports closure of significant shunts and the pulmonary vascular contraindication that guides either surgical or transcatheter repair.

treatments/2.description: Surgical repair remains a valid closure strategy, especially when anatomy is unsuitable for device closure or when the defect is primum, sinus venosus, or coronary sinus type.

evidence.snippet: Pericardial or synthetic patch closure is preferred over a direct suture, and generally completely terminates the shunt.
evidence.explanation: The review directly supports surgical patch closure as a means of terminating the interatrial shunt.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Surgical closure terminates the interatrial shunt when device closure is anatomically unsuitable or when associated anatomy requires repair.

evidence.snippet: Medical and procedural therapy for arrhythmias should consider type and timing of ASD repair.
evidence.explanation: The arrhythmia review supports individualized medical and procedural rhythm management in relation to ASD anatomy and repair timing.

treatments/3.description: Established atrial tachyarrhythmias require rhythm-specific medical or procedural management. In selected patients, ablation before or at closure can be considered because defect closure alone does not reliably eliminate an established arrhythmogenic substrate.

evidence.snippet: Atrial septal defects call for tertiary expertise where all options may be considered, namely catheter vs. surgical closure, consideration of pre-closure ablation for patients with atrial tachycardia and suitability for closure or/and targeted therapy for patients with PAH.
evidence.explanation: The adult ASD review explicitly supports considering pre-closure ablation in patients with atrial tachycardia.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Ablation interrupts the re-entrant or focal electrical circuits that manifest on the substrate of ASD-related atrial remodeling.

evidence.snippet: Studies applied variable PH definitions.
evidence.explanation: Heterogeneous definitions limit direct comparison and threshold inference across closure cohorts.

evidence.snippet: Larger, prospective studies with consistent PH definitions using the recommended measurement modality are warranted.
evidence.explanation: The meta-analysis explicitly calls for prospective, consistently measured studies to resolve this management gap.

open_questions/0.rationale: This decision separates potentially reversible shunt-associated pulmonary hypertension from severe irreversible disease and Eisenmenger physiology. Existing observational studies use heterogeneous pulmonary-hypertension definitions, so a single pressure estimate is not an adequate closure rule.

evidence.snippet: Arrhythmia incidence is decreased after ASD closure, but remains elevated compared to general population.
evidence.explanation: Persistent excess rhythm risk after closure motivates surveillance and prevention research.

evidence.snippet: However, consensus regarding frequency and duration of follow-up after device closure is lacking.
evidence.explanation: The review explicitly identifies uncertainty about post-device follow-up.

open_questions/1.rationale: Closure reduces shunt load but does not erase pre-existing atrial remodeling, and follow-up intensity varies with age at closure, residual lesions, pulmonary pressure, and rhythm history.

evidence.snippet: most secundum ASDs occur sporadically
evidence.explanation: This directly supports the gap between rare familial genes and the much larger sporadic population.

evidence.snippet: Currently, it points to different pathways and gene networks relevant to the dysregulation of cardiomyogenesis and ASD pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: The current review supports a heterogeneous network architecture rather than one dominant ASD gene.

open_questions/2.rationale: A few stable gene associations explain rare families or syndromic disease, but most secundum ASD is sporadic and a negative current panel cannot exclude a genetic contribution.

evidence.snippet: Preliminary results are limited but promising.

evidence.snippet: The objective of this project is to study the feasibility, efficacy and safety of the Optimus stent in this newly developed transcatheter procedure, in comparison with the gold-standard surgical method.

open_questions/3.rationale: Covered-stent correction is emerging, but dedicated comparative evidence and long-term data remain limited; anatomy also constrains feasibility.

evidence.snippet: BRAF mutations confers a poor prognosis in Western CRC patients, particularly in metastatic CRC (mCRC) and its mutations occur in approximately 4-20% CRC, with the vast majority being the V600E hotspot mutation.
evidence.explanation: This abstract links BRAF mutations in CRC to the V600E hotspot and supports the relevance of V600E in colorectal cancer.

evidence.snippet: BRAF V600E indicates poor prognosis in advanced colorectal cancer
evidence.explanation: CIViC's accepted assertion supports BRAF V600E as a clinically meaningful colorectal cancer driver associated with poor outcome.

steps/1.description: The V600E mutation substitutes glutamic acid for valine at position 600 in the activation segment of BRAF kinase. This mimics phosphorylation-induced activation, locking BRAF in an active conformation. The mutant kinase signals constitutively through MEK and ERK without upstream RAS activation.

steps/2.description: BRAF V600E-mutant CRC commonly develops through sessile serrated lesions rather than the classic APC-driven adenoma-carcinoma sequence. Constitutive MAPK signaling cooperates with widespread CpG island methylation to silence tumor suppressor loci, creating a CIMP-high intermediate state that can progress through either an MSI-H or MSS trajectory.

steps/3.description: Constitutive BRAF V600E activation leads to continuous phosphorylation of MEK1/2, which phosphorylates ERK1/2. Activated ERK translocates to the nucleus and drives expression of genes promoting cell proliferation, survival, and invasion. This signaling is independent of growth factor receptor activation.

steps/4.description: Sustained ERK signaling promotes entry into the cell cycle by inducing cyclin D1 and other proliferative genes while suppressing cell cycle inhibitors. This drives continuous tumor cell division independent of external growth signals.

steps/5.description: In approximately half of BRAF V600E CRCs, CIMP-high methylation silences MLH1, producing mismatch-repair deficiency and high microsatellite instability. This branch is usually sporadic rather than Lynch syndrome-associated and creates a more immunogenic tumor phenotype that can respond to immune checkpoint blockade.

steps/6.description: Unlike melanoma, colorectal cancer cells have high EGFR expression. When BRAF is inhibited, relief of ERK-mediated negative feedback leads to rapid EGFR reactivation, which signals through RAS and CRAF to restore MAPK pathway activity. This explains why BRAF inhibitor monotherapy fails in colorectal cancer but works in melanoma.

steps/7.description: Resistance to BRAF/EGFR-targeted therapy is often polyclonal and converges on renewed MAPK signaling. Reported escape mechanisms include amplification of EGFR, KRAS, or mutant BRAF, acquired KRAS or MAP2K1 mutations, and MET alterations; baseline TP53 mutation has been associated with acquired MET amplification.

edges/2.description: BRAF V600E initiates a serrated precursor pathway with epigenetic silencing

The MSI-H branch is more immunogenic because mismatch-repair deficiency increases neoantigen load, though BRAF V600E still carries adverse prognostic implications within MSI-H CRC.

treatments/4.description: Surgery for localized disease or oligometastatic disease in selected patients. Adjuvant chemotherapy is standard for stage III disease, though BRAF-mutant tumors may have attenuated benefit.

evidence.snippet: High microsatellite instability (MSI-H) colorectal cancer (CRC), caused by deficient mismatch repair, accounts for about 15% of all CRC cases and is more common in right-sided tumors.
evidence.explanation: This abstract explicitly links MSI-H CRC to deficient mismatch repair, supporting the core disease mechanism described.

steps/0.description: Loss of MMR protein function (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2) impairs the recognition and repair of DNA replication errors. The MMR system normally corrects base-base mismatches and insertion/deletion loops at microsatellite sequences. Deficiency leads to accumulation of thousands of somatic mutations.

evidence.snippet: Microsatellite unstable (MSI) colorectal cancers (CRCs) are due to DNA mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency
evidence.explanation: Abstract links MSI CRC to MMR deficiency, supporting the MSI mechanism.

steps/1.description: Microsatellites are repetitive DNA sequences highly susceptible to replication errors. Without functional MMR, these sequences accumulate insertions and deletions, detectable as length variations (instability) compared to normal tissue. MSI-H is defined as instability at two or more of five standard markers.

evidence.snippet: The pathogenic alterations of MMR genes lead to the accumulation of frequent somatic mutational events
evidence.explanation: Abstract notes frequent somatic mutational events from MMR alterations, consistent with hypermutation.

evidence.snippet: Mutational analysis of the tumor specimens by next-generation sequencing confirmed microsatellite instability in all 14 patients for whom testing was performed and revealed a high tumor mutational burden, ranging from 37.9 to 103.0 mutations per megabase (mean, 60.0).
evidence.explanation: Next-generation sequencing of mismatch repair-deficient tumors directly quantified a high tumor mutational burden (mean 60 mutations per megabase), supporting the hypermutated, high-TMB phenotype of MSI-H disease.

steps/2.description: MSI-H tumors accumulate 10-100 times more somatic mutations than microsatellite stable tumors, resulting in tumor mutational burden often exceeding 10-20 mutations per megabase. This creates abundant neoantigens derived from mutant peptides presented on MHC molecules.

evidence.snippet: these tumours arbour a high antigen burden and are highly infiltrated with cytotoxic T-cell lymphocytes
evidence.explanation: MMR-deficient colorectal cancers carry a high antigen (neoantigen) burden and are densely infiltrated by cytotoxic T lymphocytes, supporting the neoantigen-driven anti-tumor immune response.

steps/3.description: The high neoantigen burden in MSI-H tumors stimulates robust anti-tumor immunity. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, particularly CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, recognize and attack tumor cells presenting neoantigens. However, tumors upregulate PD-L1 as an adaptive resistance mechanism.

steps/4.description: Coding microsatellites in tumor suppressor genes (TGFbetaRII, BAX, ACVR2, IGF2R) accumulate frameshift mutations, inactivating their tumor suppressive functions. TGFbetaRII frameshift is particularly common, disrupting TGF-beta growth inhibition.

evidence.snippet: Tumor samples evaluated by multiplex quantitative immunofluorescence analysis showed variable PD-L1 protein expression with higher levels in cytokeratin-negative stromal cells than in cytokeratin-expressing cancer cells, as well as lymphocytic infiltration enriched for cells expressing CD8 or CD20.
evidence.explanation: Quantitative immunofluorescence of mismatch repair-deficient tumors demonstrated PD-L1 protein expression together with CD8+ T-lymphocyte infiltration, consistent with adaptive PD-L1 upregulation in an immunogenic microenvironment.

steps/5.description: MSI-H tumors upregulate PD-L1 expression in response to interferon-gamma from infiltrating T cells. PD-L1 engagement of PD-1 on T cells suppresses cytotoxic function, allowing immune evasion despite the immunogenic microenvironment. This makes MSI-H tumors vulnerable to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade.

genes/2.notes: MSH6 germline mutations cause Lynch syndrome with attenuated phenotype and later age of onset.

genes/3.notes: PMS2 germline mutations cause Lynch syndrome with lower penetrance than MLH1/MSH2 mutations.

evidence.snippet: They are thought to arise from an anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction, which are congenital anomalies between pancreatic and bile ducts.
evidence.explanation: Establishes anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction as the congenital lesion from which these cysts are thought to arise.

steps/0.description: The initiating congenital lesion. The pancreatic and common bile ducts join outside the duodenal wall, producing an abnormally long common channel that lies beyond the sphincter of Oddi. The sphincter therefore cannot regulate the junction, and the two duct systems communicate freely.

evidence.snippet: A reflux of pancreatic contents into the cyst due to long common channel is likely to worsen the pathology further.
evidence.explanation: States the reflux of pancreatic contents driven by the long common channel, which is the mechanism this node describes.

steps/1.description: Because hydrostatic pressure in the pancreatic duct exceeds that in the bile duct, activated pancreatic enzymes reflux persistently into the biliary tree. This is the mechanistic bridge between the anatomical anomaly and the tissue damage that follows.

evidence.snippet: ICCP inversely correlated with cyst wall changes (P = 0.003, 0.0001, 0.023, 0.0013, respectively)
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the cyst wall ulceration, inflammation, fibrosis and metaplasia that constitute this injury, and shows they are worst in the low-pressure maljunction cysts.

steps/2.description: The convergent tissue lesion. Refluxed pancreatic enzymes, bile stasis and raised intraductal bile-acid concentration injure the biliary epithelium repeatedly. Cyst wall histology shows ulceration, inflammation, fibrosis and metaplasia, and this node is the branch point from which both the dilatation and the carcinogenic sequence follow.

evidence.snippet: Pathological findings strongly suggest a hyperplasia-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence in carcinogenesis of pancreatico-biliary maljunction (PBM).
evidence.explanation: Names the hyperplasia-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence in maljunction directly, which is exactly what this node asserts.

evidence.snippet: the TP53 mutation rates in the epithelium of control patients, epithelium of PBM patients without GBC, peritumoral mucosa of GBC patients with PBM, and tumor tissue of GBC patients with PBM were 10, 10, 38, and 75%, respectively (p <  0.01)
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the stepwise molecular accumulation along that sequence.

steps/3.description: The clinically decisive consequence. Repeated injury and repair drive epithelial hyperplasia, then dysplasia, then carcinoma, with TP53 alteration accumulating stepwise along the maljunction-to-carcinoma axis. This is why the condition is treated as premalignant and excised rather than drained, and why surveillance continues for decades after operation.

evidence.snippet: High pressure cysts had normal pancreaticobiliary junction.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the maljunction cases this entry models are the low-pressure ones, which is why pressure is not invoked as the driver of dilatation.

steps/4.description: The defining anatomical lesion and the reason the condition is named as it is. The pressure relationship is counterintuitive and worth stating explicitly: intracystic pressure correlates inversely with cyst volume and inversely with common channel length, and high-pressure cysts were those with a normal pancreaticobiliary junction. The maljunction cysts modelled here are therefore the low-pressure, high-volume, high-amylase ones, in which enzyme exposure rather than raised pressure damages the wall; raised pressure instead tracks with hepatic parenchymal injury.

steps/5.description: Clinical endpoint. Cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinoma arise in the affected biliary epithelium.
