treatments/3.description: Genetic counseling is recommended for affected families. Most CINCA/NOMID cases arise from de novo mutations, but germline transmission is possible. Assessment of recurrence risk, somatic mosaicism implications, and reproductive options should be discussed.

hypotheses/0.description: Gain-of-function NLRP3 mutations cause constitutive inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 activation, driving excessive IL-1beta production as the central effector of systemic and organ-specific inflammation. The dominant pathogenic role of IL-1beta is established by the rapid, near-complete clinical and biochemical response to IL-1 blockade.

evidence.snippet: In 40% (4/10) of the cohort a post-zygotic NLRP3 mutation leading to somatic mosaicism was found by ADS.
evidence.explanation: Even with amplicon-based deep sequencing, only 40% of mutation-negative CAPS patients were resolved as NLRP3 mosaics, leaving the majority genetically unexplained.

open_questions/0.rationale: Deep/amplicon sequencing reclassifies many "mutation-negative" cases as low-level NLRP3 mosaicism, but a substantial fraction still has no detectable NLRP3 variant even with the most sensitive methods, yet responds to IL-1 blockade exactly like genotype-positive patients. The genetic lesion in this residual group — deeper mosaicism below detection, a non-coding/regulatory NLRP3 change, or a variant in another inflammasome gene — is unresolved, leaving the first step of the causal chain unaccounted for in these patients.

evidence.snippet: there were significant differences between twins in phenotype severity, suggestive of epigenetic differences and/or involvement of environmental factors.
evidence.explanation: Phenotypic discordance between monozygotic CINCA twins implicates epigenetic/environmental modifiers of severity beyond the shared NLRP3 genotype.

open_questions/1.rationale: CINCA/NOMID shows variable expressivity even for the same NLRP3 change, and monozygotic twins concordant for the genotype can diverge markedly in severity. This points to epigenetic and/or environmental modifiers shaping the phenotype, which are currently unidentified and limit genotype-based prognostication.

evidence.snippet: A state of severe retinal dystrophy of post-inflammatory origin became evident on funduscopy, optical coherence tomography and visual electrophysiology tests at the age of 10 years, which remained stationary after 1 year of anakinra treatment.
evidence.explanation: Established post-inflammatory retinal dystrophy persisted unchanged after a year of anakinra, illustrating that fixed neurosensory damage may not reverse with IL-1 blockade.

open_questions/2.rationale: IL-1 blockade reliably controls active inflammation and can improve MRI-visible cochlear and leptomeningeal lesions, but fixed post-inflammatory damage such as retinal dystrophy can remain stationary despite treatment. Whether any established neurosensory injury is recoverable — versus only preventable by very early treatment — is unresolved and is central to the rationale for early diagnosis before genetic confirmation.

steps/5.description: Failed COPA/SURF4-mediated retrieval traps ER-resident STING at the Golgi, where it multimerises and undergoes ligand-independent activation with TBK1 phosphorylation. evidence.snippet: CTD COPA mutations result in disease by increased ER stress, disturbed intracellular transport, and increased proinﬂammatory signaling.
evidence.explanation: Delafontaine et al. summarise the CTD mechanism as ER stress plus increased proinflammatory (NF-kappaB) signalling.

evidence.snippet: Immunological features involve autoantibody formation, elevated expression of IL-1β and IL-6, and increase in the number of Th17 cells.
evidence.explanation: Kumrah et al. describe the elevated IL-1beta and IL-6 cytokine profile expected from NF-kappaB activation, linking it to TH17 expansion in patients.

steps/8.description: Sustained ER stress and Golgi-localised STING signalling activate canonical NF-kappaB and induce IL-1beta, IL-6, and other proinflammatory cytokines that amplify autoinflammation. NF-kappaB activation is most prominently demonstrated in CTD variant cells.

evidence.snippet: Patient-derived CD4(+) T cells also demonstrate significant skewing toward a TH17 phenotype that is implicated in autoimmunity.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived T-cell data provide direct evidence of TH17-biased adaptive immune activation in COPA syndrome.

evidence.snippet: All but 1 patient tested positive for autoantibodies, and increased interferon signalling was noted in all those tested.
evidence.explanation: Large cohort data confirm the characteristic combination of autoantibody positivity and interferon activation in clinically affected patients.

steps/9.description: Sustained type I interferon signalling, ER stress, and IL-6/IL-1beta output skew CD4+ T cells toward a TH17 fate, drive B-cell autoantibody production, and produce the autoimmune cytokine milieu underlying chronic injury in lung, joint, and kidney tissues.

evidence.snippet: The most prevalent imaging finding of COPA syndrome is diffuse lung disease related to early childhood-onset recurrent pulmonary hemorrhage and lymphoid hyperplasia that may progress to pulmonary fibrosis.
evidence.explanation: Imaging cohort confirms that the dominant clinical manifestation is lung-targeted autoimmune injury, with progression to fibrosis.

evidence.snippet: Kidney involvement was heterogenous between patients (ANCA-associated vasculitis-like disease, lupus or immune-complex mediated glomerulonephritis or overlapping phenotypes), and all had advanced histological damage at clinical presentation.
evidence.explanation: Renal histology in COPA syndrome shows multiple immune-mediated glomerulonephritis patterns consistent with autoimmune end-organ injury.

steps/10.description: Convergent type I interferon, NF-kappaB, and TH17/autoantibody output targets the lung (interstitial pneumonia, capillaritis, alveolar haemorrhage, lymphoid hyperplasia), the synovium (inflammatory arthritis), and the kidney (ANCA-associated, lupus-like or immune-complex glomerulonephritis), and is the proximate driver of the clinical phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Pulmonary involvement was observed in 34 patients, with interstitial lung disease in most cases (n = 31) and diffuse alveolar haemorrhage in 11 individuals.
evidence.explanation: Multicenter European cohort confirms interstitial lung disease as the most common organ manifestation; 31/38 symptomatic patients had ILD, which is 82% and falls in the VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/11.description: Pulmonary disease is the dominant organ manifestation and is most often an interstitial lung disease pattern.

evidence.snippet: Pulmonary involvement was observed in 34 patients, with interstitial lung disease in most cases (n = 31) and diffuse alveolar haemorrhage in 11 individuals.
evidence.explanation: The same cohort explicitly documents diffuse alveolar hemorrhage as a core pulmonary feature; 11/38 symptomatic patients had diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, which is 29% and falls in the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/12.description: Alveolar hemorrhage may be clinically overt or insidious and is a distinctive pulmonary complication of COPA syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Onset is usually in early childhood, with unique disease features including alveolar hemorrhage, which can be insidious, pulmonary cyst formation, and progressive pulmonary fibrosis in nonspecific interstitial pneumonia or lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia patterns.
evidence.explanation: Review abstract identifies progressive pulmonary fibrosis as a distinctive pulmonary manifestation within the COPA syndrome ILD spectrum.

steps/13.description: Progressive pulmonary fibrosis can develop within the interstitial lung disease spectrum of COPA syndrome, including nonspecific interstitial pneumonia and lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia patterns.

evidence.snippet: Onset is usually in early childhood, with unique disease features including alveolar hemorrhage, which can be insidious, pulmonary cyst formation, and progressive pulmonary fibrosis in nonspecific interstitial pneumonia or lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia patterns.
evidence.explanation: Review abstract identifies pulmonary cyst formation as a characteristic COPA syndrome lung feature.

steps/14.description: Cystic lung changes are a recognized pulmonary feature of COPA syndrome and may accompany chronic interstitial lung disease.

evidence.snippet: Twenty-six patients demonstrated joint involvement, and 7 had documented kidney disease.
evidence.explanation: Cohort data show that inflammatory joint involvement is common among symptomatic patients; 26/38 affected individuals had joint involvement, which is 68% and falls in the FREQUENT band.

steps/15.description: Inflammatory joint disease is a common extrapulmonary manifestation and can precede or accompany lung disease.

evidence.snippet: Kidney involvement was heterogenous between patients (ANCA-associated vasculitis-like disease, lupus or immune-complex mediated glomerulonephritis or overlapping phenotypes), and all had advanced histological damage at clinical presentation.
evidence.explanation: Kidney transplant case series demonstrates that glomerulonephritis is part of the renal disease spectrum in COPA syndrome.

steps/16.description: Immune-mediated kidney disease occurs in a subset of patients and may present as ANCA-associated, lupus-like, or immune-complex glomerulonephritis.

evidence.snippet: The most prevalent imaging finding of COPA syndrome is diffuse lung disease related to early childhood-onset recurrent pulmonary hemorrhage and lymphoid hyperplasia that may progress to pulmonary fibrosis.
evidence.explanation: Pediatric imaging cohort identifies pulmonary lymphoid hyperplasia as a defining component of COPA syndrome lung disease.

steps/17.description: Florid pulmonary lymphoid hyperplasia, often manifesting on biopsy as follicular bronchiolitis or lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia, is a characteristic histopathological feature of COPA syndrome lung disease.

evidence.snippet: All 12 had abnormal chest CT exams, with findings including ground-glass opacities (12/12), cysts (8/12), septal thickening (9/12), nodules (8/12), fibrosis (7/12), crazy-paving (2/12), consolidation (1/12), hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy (11/12), and chest wall deformity (5/12).
evidence.explanation: Hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy was present on chest CT in 11/12 (~92%) of pediatric COPA patients, supporting VERY_FREQUENT classification.

steps/18.description: Hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy is a near-universal radiologic finding in pediatric COPA syndrome and reflects the lymphoproliferative aspect of pulmonary disease.

evidence.snippet: All 12 had abnormal chest CT exams, with findings including ground-glass opacities (12/12), cysts (8/12), septal thickening (9/12), nodules (8/12), fibrosis (7/12), crazy-paving (2/12), consolidation (1/12), hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy (11/12), and chest wall deformity (5/12).
evidence.explanation: Ground-glass opacification was seen in 12/12 (100%) of pediatric patients on chest CT.

steps/19.description: Ground-glass opacification is the most consistent chest CT finding in COPA syndrome and reflects diffuse alveolar inflammation, hemorrhage, and lymphoid infiltration.

evidence.snippet: All 12 had abnormal chest CT exams, with findings including ground-glass opacities (12/12), cysts (8/12), septal thickening (9/12), nodules (8/12), fibrosis (7/12), crazy-paving (2/12), consolidation (1/12), hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy (11/12), and chest wall deformity (5/12).
evidence.explanation: Pulmonary nodules were detected in 8/12 patients on chest CT in the imaging cohort.

steps/20.description: Pulmonary nodules are a recurrent CT finding in COPA syndrome and may correspond to lymphoid follicles or inflammatory foci that improve on immunosuppression.

evidence.snippet: All 12 had abnormal chest CT exams, with findings including ground-glass opacities (12/12), cysts (8/12), septal thickening (9/12), nodules (8/12), fibrosis (7/12), crazy-paving (2/12), consolidation (1/12), hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy (11/12), and chest wall deformity (5/12).
evidence.explanation: A crazy-paving pattern was identified in 2/12 patients on chest CT, supporting it as a recognised but less common COPA syndrome finding.

steps/21.description: A crazy-paving pattern (combined ground-glass opacification with superimposed septal thickening) can occur in COPA syndrome, often reflecting alveolar hemorrhage or organizing pneumonia.

evidence.snippet: Four had musculoskeletal imaging revealing synovitis (2/4), bone erosions (1/4), tenosynovitis (1/4), enthesitis (1/4), and subcutaneous nodules (1/4).
evidence.explanation: Musculoskeletal MRI in COPA syndrome documents synovitis as the dominant inflammatory finding.

steps/22.description: Active inflammatory synovitis can be detected by MRI in COPA syndrome arthritis, supporting an inflammatory rather than mechanical pathophysiology.

evidence.snippet: All subjects were positive for anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, anti-nuclear antibody or both and 71% of subjects had rheumatoid factor positivity.
evidence.explanation: International cohort confirms ANA (with or without ANCA) in all subjects, supporting ANA positivity as a defining serologic feature.

steps/23.description: Antinuclear antibodies are common in COPA syndrome and contribute to diagnostic confusion with juvenile systemic lupus erythematosus or juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

evidence.snippet: All subjects were positive for anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, anti-nuclear antibody or both and 71% of subjects had rheumatoid factor positivity.
evidence.explanation: International COPA cohort documents ANCA positivity (with or without ANA) in all subjects.

steps/24.description: Cytoplasmic and perinuclear ANCA positivity is common and contributes to ANCA-associated vasculitis-like renal and pulmonary phenotypes in COPA syndrome.

evidence.snippet: All subjects were positive for anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, anti-nuclear antibody or both and 71% of subjects had rheumatoid factor positivity.
evidence.explanation: 71% RF positivity in the international pulmonary cohort places this within the FREQUENT band.

steps/25.description: Rheumatoid factor is positive in a majority of patients and frequently leads to misdiagnosis as juvenile idiopathic arthritis or rheumatoid arthritis before genetic testing.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of peripheral blood showed activation of type 1 interferon pathway, which was also confirmed in 4 previously reported COPA patients.
evidence.explanation: Volpi et al. demonstrate type I interferon pathway activation as a peripheral blood signature confirmed across multiple COPA syndrome cases.

steps/26.description: A peripheral blood type I interferon signature is a defining immunological feature of COPA syndrome and is mechanistically driven by Golgi-localised STING activation.

evidence.snippet: Patient-derived CD4(+) T cells also demonstrate significant skewing toward a TH17 phenotype that is implicated in autoimmunity.
evidence.explanation: Watkin et al. directly demonstrate TH17 skewing in patient-derived CD4 T cells.

steps/27.description: Patient-derived CD4+ T cells show skewing toward a TH17 phenotype with elevated IL-1beta, IL-6 and IL-17 cytokine output, contributing to autoimmune end-organ inflammation.

evidence.snippet: The most common pulmonary findings included cysts on chest computed tomography and evidence of follicular bronchiolitis on lung biopsy.
evidence.explanation: Tsui et al. identify follicular bronchiolitis on lung biopsy as one of the most common pulmonary findings in the international COPA cohort.

steps/28.description: Follicular bronchiolitis is a histopathologic hallmark of COPA syndrome pulmonary disease, identified on lung biopsy and reflecting the underlying lymphoproliferative response in airways.

evidence.snippet: Previously undescribed features included skin (n = 12), cardiac (n = 8), gastrointestinal (n = 7), and hepatic involvement (n = 5).
evidence.explanation: Skin involvement was reported in 12/38 (32%) symptomatic patients in the European cohort, supporting FREQUENT classification.

steps/29.description: Skin manifestations are now recognised as a previously underappreciated feature of COPA syndrome, present in roughly one-third of symptomatic patients in the largest published cohort.

evidence.snippet: Previously undescribed features included skin (n = 12), cardiac (n = 8), gastrointestinal (n = 7), and hepatic involvement (n = 5).
evidence.explanation: Cardiac involvement was reported in 8/38 (21%) symptomatic patients in the European cohort, falling within the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/30.description: Cardiac involvement is an emerging extrapulmonary manifestation of COPA syndrome, reported in roughly one in five symptomatic patients in the largest cohort to date.

evidence.snippet: Previously undescribed features included skin (n = 12), cardiac (n = 8), gastrointestinal (n = 7), and hepatic involvement (n = 5).
evidence.explanation: Gastrointestinal involvement was reported in 7/38 (18%) symptomatic patients, within the OCCASIONAL band.

steps/31.description: Gastrointestinal manifestations are now recognised in COPA syndrome and contribute to the multisystem phenotype, particularly in symptomatic children.

evidence.snippet: Previously undescribed features included skin (n = 12), cardiac (n = 8), gastrointestinal (n = 7), and hepatic involvement (n = 5).
evidence.explanation: Hepatic involvement was reported in 5/38 (13%) symptomatic patients, within the OCCASIONAL band; this complements earlier descriptions of unexplained transaminitis (PMID:32970305).

steps/32.description: Liver involvement (which can include unexplained transaminitis) is a recognised but uncommon manifestation of COPA syndrome, present in around one in eight symptomatic patients.

evidence.snippet: We identified four unique deleterious variants in the COPA gene (encoding coatomer subunit α) affecting the same functional domain.
evidence.explanation: Original family-based genetic study establishes COPA as the causative disease gene with WD40 domain variants.

evidence.snippet: We described 3 heterozygous mutations in the C-terminal domain (CTD) of COPA (p.C1013S, p.R1058C, and p.R1142X) in 6 children from 3 unrelated families with a similar syndrome of autoinflammation and autoimmunity.
evidence.explanation: Delafontaine et al. expand the COPA mutational spectrum to include CTD variants.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous pathogenic COPA variants are the cause of COPA syndrome. Classical disease variants are missense changes in the N-terminal WD40 cargo-recognition domain (recurrent residues include Lys230, Arg233, Glu241, Asp243, and Val242), which impair binding of dilysine ER-retrieval cargo. A second variant class affects the C-terminal domain (e.g., p.Cys1013Ser, p.Arg1058Cys, p.Arg1142X) and disrupts COPI integrity, producing a clinically similar but mechanistically distinct phenotype.

evidence.snippet: We show that the common HAQ STING allele mediates complete clinical protection.
evidence.explanation: Co-segregation analysis of 35 COPA variant carriers establishes HAQ STING as a dominant clinical modifier.

evidence.snippet: we found that HAQ STING acts dominantly to dampen COPA-dependent STING signaling.
evidence.explanation: Cellular experiments confirm the dominant suppressive mechanism of HAQ STING on COPA-dependent STING signalling.

genes/1.notes: STING1 is not a causal COPA syndrome gene. The common HAQ STING haplotype (R71H/G230A/R293Q in STING1) is represented here only as a dominant protective modifier: when co-inherited with a pathogenic COPA variant, HAQ STING dampens STING signalling and provides complete clinical protection. It accounts for much of the ~15-20% nonpenetrance observed in COPA syndrome families and motivates STING-directed gene therapy strategies.

evidence.snippet: Twenty-two patients were treated with Janus kinase inhibitors with promising efficacy.
evidence.explanation: Large European cohort provides the strongest available abstract-level support for JAK inhibitor use in COPA syndrome.

evidence.snippet: JAK inhibitor therapy seems to be the most promising therapeutic choice now.
evidence.explanation: 2024 review highlights JAK inhibition as the leading current therapeutic strategy.

evidence.snippet: Baricitinib treatment in children with COPA syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Matucci-Cerinic et al. report a pediatric case series of baricitinib (a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor) in children with COPA syndrome, supporting the JAK inhibitor class for pediatric disease. The PubMed record is a letter without a structured abstract, so the canonical title is used as the reference statement.

treatments/0.description: JAK inhibitors block JAK-STAT signalling downstream of the type I interferon receptor and are the most promising mechanism-targeted therapy in COPA syndrome. Evidence level: observational cohort and review-level support, with published cohort-level evidence supporting baricitinib and ruxolitinib for both interstitial lung disease and arthritis.

evidence.snippet: All subjects received immunosuppressive therapy.
evidence.explanation: Tsui et al. report that all subjects in the international pulmonary cohort received immunosuppressive therapy as standard care.

treatments/1.description: Standard induction for severe alveolar hemorrhage uses systemic glucocorticoids combined with cyclophosphamide, with subsequent maintenance using mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine. Evidence level: case series/observational standard care. Radiographic improvement is common but pulmonary function may continue to decline.

evidence.snippet: Two out of four patients required lung transplantation due to intractable interstitial lung disease and respiratory failure.
evidence.explanation: Case report documents lung transplantation as a treatment option for end-stage COPA syndrome interstitial lung disease unresponsive to immunosuppression.

treatments/2.description: Lung transplantation is offered to patients with end-stage progressive interstitial lung disease refractory to immunosuppression and JAK inhibition. Evidence level: case reports/literature review for end-stage COPA lung disease, with allograft dysfunction reported.

evidence.snippet: Kidney involvement was heterogenous between patients (ANCA-associated vasculitis-like disease, lupus or immune-complex mediated glomerulonephritis or overlapping phenotypes), and all had advanced histological damage at clinical presentation.
evidence.explanation: Case series describes five COPA syndrome patients with advanced renal histology presenting for kidney transplant evaluation.

treatments/3.description: Patients who progress to advanced glomerular damage and end-stage renal disease require kidney transplantation, with outcomes documented in a multi-patient case series. Evidence level: five-patient observational case series.

evidence.snippet: Expressing HAQ STING in patient cells rescued the molecular phenotype of COPA syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Cellular rescue with HAQ STING establishes proof-of-concept for STING-directed gene therapy, framed as "a potential universal gene therapy approach for patients."

treatments/4.description: Direct STING pathway inhibition (e.g., small-molecule inhibitors such as H-151) and STING1-directed gene therapy aimed at introducing the protective HAQ allele are emerging upstream therapeutic strategies based on the central role of Golgi-localised STING activation in COPA syndrome. Evidence level: experimental/preclinical, with BI 3000202 now in Phase 1 safety and tolerability testing for selected type I interferonopathies including COPA syndrome.

evidence.snippet: COX5A is a nuclear-encoded subunit of mitochondrial respiratory chain complex IV
evidence.explanation: Establishes COX5A as a nuclear-encoded structural subunit of Complex IV, the protein lost in this disorder.

evidence.snippet: the variant lies within the evolutionarily conserved COX5A/COX4 interface domain, suggesting that it alters the interaction between these two subunits during complex IV biogenesis
evidence.explanation: Localizes the lesion to the COX5A/COX4 interface, the structural basis for impaired Complex IV biogenesis.

evidence.snippet: The monomeric COX1 assembly intermediate accumulates demonstrating a function of COX5A in complex IV biogenesis
evidence.explanation: Accumulation of the monomeric COX1 assembly intermediate in patient cells demonstrates a stalled, failed assembly.

steps/1.description: Biallelic COX5A variants disrupt a nuclear-encoded structural subunit of Complex IV. The reported variant lies within the conserved COX5A/COX4 interface domain, altering the interaction between these subunits during holoenzyme biogenesis. As a result the monomeric COX1 assembly intermediate accumulates and the mature enzyme fails to assemble, yielding isolated Complex IV biogenesis failure.

evidence.snippet: the enzymatic activity and protein levels of complex IV and several of its subunits are reduced
evidence.explanation: Reduced Complex IV enzymatic activity and protein levels establish the functional terminal-electron-transfer deficit.

steps/2.description: Reduced amounts and activity of assembled Complex IV block electron transfer from cytochrome c to oxygen and proton pumping, collapsing oxidative ATP synthesis. In COX5A-deficient patient fibroblasts the enzymatic activity and protein levels of Complex IV and several of its subunits are reduced.

evidence.snippet: early-onset pulmonary arterial hypertension, lactic acidemia, failure to thrive, and isolated complex IV deficiency
evidence.explanation: Lactic acidemia in the affected siblings is the metabolic consequence of failed oxidative ATP synthesis.

steps/3.description: With oxidative phosphorylation impaired, pyruvate is shunted to lactate, elevating blood lactate; in COX5A-related disease this presented as lactic acidemia in both affected siblings.

evidence.snippet: early-onset pulmonary arterial hypertension, lactic acidemia, failure to thrive, and isolated complex IV deficiency
evidence.explanation: Early-onset pulmonary arterial hypertension and failure to thrive are the high-energy-tissue manifestations of the bioenergetic deficit.

steps/4.description: The bioenergetic deficit manifests in high-demand tissues. In COX5A-related disease the dominant organ phenotype is early-onset pulmonary arterial hypertension, accompanied by failure to thrive, distinguishing it from the encephalopathy/cardiomyopathy presentations of other nuclear COX deficiencies.

evidence.snippet: early-onset pulmonary arterial hypertension, lactic acidemia, failure to thrive, and isolated complex IV deficiency
evidence.explanation: The affected siblings presented with early-onset pulmonary arterial hypertension.

steps/5.description: Early-onset pulmonary arterial hypertension, the dominant presenting feature of COX5A-related Complex IV deficiency in the two reported siblings.

evidence.snippet: early-onset pulmonary arterial hypertension, lactic acidemia, failure to thrive, and isolated complex IV deficiency
evidence.explanation: Lactic acidemia was present in the affected siblings.

steps/6.description: Lactic acidemia (elevated blood lactate), a presenting metabolic feature of COX5A-related Complex IV deficiency.

evidence.snippet: early-onset pulmonary arterial hypertension, lactic acidemia, failure to thrive, and isolated complex IV deficiency
evidence.explanation: Failure to thrive was a presenting feature in the affected siblings.

steps/7.description: Failure to thrive accompanied the pulmonary arterial hypertension and lactic acidemia in the affected siblings.

edges/1.description: Failure to assemble Complex IV yields a catalytically deficient holoenzyme.

edges/2.description: Loss of oxidative ATP synthesis forces anaerobic glycolysis and lactate accumulation.

edges/3.description: The bioenergetic deficit injures high-demand tissues, including the pulmonary vasculature.

edges/4.description: Lactate overproduction manifests clinically as lactic acidemia.

edges/5.description: Pulmonary vascular involvement manifests as early-onset pulmonary arterial hypertension.

edges/6.description: Systemic energy failure manifests as failure to thrive.

evidence.snippet: We present patients with a homozygous pathogenic variant in the COX5A gene
evidence.explanation: Identifies the homozygous COX5A variant as the causal lesion.

evidence.snippet: Lentiviral complementation rescues complex IV deficiency
evidence.explanation: Re-expression of wild-type COX5A rescued the biochemical defect in patient fibroblasts, confirming causality.

treatments/0.description: No curative therapy exists; management is supportive, addressing the pulmonary arterial hypertension, lactic acidemia, and failure to thrive with multidisciplinary supportive care.

evidence.snippet: copper supplementation leads to partial rescue of complex IV deficiency in patient fibroblasts
evidence.explanation: Copper supplementation partially rescued Complex IV deficiency in patient fibroblasts, identifying a potential therapeutic lead.

treatments/1.description: A preclinical therapeutic lead: copper supplementation partially rescued Complex IV deficiency in patient fibroblasts in vitro. This is an experimental finding in cells, not an established clinical therapy.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic pathogenic variants in COX6B1 have been described in four patients to date with varying disease manifestations.
evidence.explanation: The four previously reported patients precede the new fifth patient in this report; this is not a population frequency.

evidence.snippet: The novel p.Trp31Arg variant was predicted to be pathogenic in silico, and further functional analyses with biochemical analysis of mitochondrial function showed isolated COX deficiency.
evidence.explanation: The clinical report identifies p.Trp31Arg and a specific biochemical complex IV defect.

steps/1.description: Homozygous disease-associated missense variants impair COX6B1 function. The consequences include reduced protein abundance for some alleles and tissues, or impaired holoenzyme incorporation despite stable abundance for Arg20His fibroblasts.

evidence.snippet: Urea-PAGE combined with western blotting analysis of patient's muscle mitochondrial revealed a barely detectable residual amount of COX6B1 protein (11% of control normalized to SDH), suggesting that the mutant protein in highly unstable.
evidence.explanation: The Arg20Cys muscle sample retains about 11% of control COX6B1; this is severe reduction, not complete absence.

evidence.snippet: Muscle biopsy showed a specific lack of COX6B1 protein together with complex IV deficiency on western blot, enzyme histochemistry, and immuno-histochemistry.
evidence.explanation: Patient muscle shows loss of detectable COX6B1 and deficient complex IV staining.

evidence.snippet: Taken together, these results suggest that mutant COX6B1R19H was normally expressed in fibroblasts, but failed to be, or to remain, stably incorporated in the COX holocomplex.
evidence.explanation: Patient fibroblasts retain total mutant protein but have impaired stable incorporation; R19H is mature-protein numbering for p.Arg20His.

steps/2.description: COX6B1 protein is severely reduced in Arg20Cys muscle and absent by the reported Trp31Arg muscle assays. This is not universal: Arg20His fibroblasts retain total COX6B1 protein.

evidence.snippet: Taken together, these results suggest that mutant COX6B1R19H was normally expressed in fibroblasts, but failed to be, or to remain, stably incorporated in the COX holocomplex.
evidence.explanation: Patient fibroblasts retain total mutant protein but have impaired stable incorporation; R19H is mature-protein numbering for p.Arg20His.

evidence.snippet: As shown in Figure 4A, fully assembled COX was reduced to approximately 40% in mutant versus control muscle.
evidence.explanation: Native gels show reduced assembled enzyme in patient muscle, with residual holoenzyme.

steps/3.description: Arg20His mutant protein is poorly incorporated or retained in the native holoenzyme despite preserved total fibroblast abundance. Muscle holoenzyme abundance is also reduced.

evidence.snippet: Altogether, these results suggest a block in cIV assembly at the stage of MT-CO2 maturation and/or incorporation.
evidence.explanation: Knockout cells retain MT-CO1/COX4/COX5A intermediates but lose MT-CO2 and mature complex IV; direct copper transfer by COX6B1 remains unproven.

steps/4.description: COX6B1-null HEK293 cells accumulate early MT-CO1/COX4/COX5A assemblies while MT-CO2 and mature complex IV are depleted. Redox correction allows partial assembly to resume. These findings identify an early assembly role; direct COX6B1 copper-transfer chemistry is still unresolved.

evidence.snippet: As shown in Figure 4A, fully assembled COX was reduced to approximately 40% in mutant versus control muscle.
evidence.explanation: Native gels show reduced assembled enzyme in patient muscle, with residual holoenzyme.

evidence.snippet: These experiments showed the total loss of fully assembled monomeric cIV (IV), cIV dimer (IV2), as well as SC III2IV in 6B1KO.
evidence.explanation: Complete absence of these native forms is a result of engineered knockout; patient missense alleles can retain holoenzyme.

steps/5.description: Impaired assembly and stability reduce mature cytochrome c oxidase. Arg20His patient muscle retains about 40% of control assembled enzyme, whereas complete knockout cells lose detectable monomer, dimer and III2IV forms.

evidence.snippet: The enzymatic analysis of mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes in muscle mitochondria revealed undetectable COX (complex IV) activity, whereas complexes I, II and II+III were within the normal limit.
evidence.explanation: The Arg20Cys patient has an isolated muscle complex IV defect; other measured respiratory complexes are preserved.

evidence.snippet: Evaluation of the “bioenergetic phenotype,” i.e., the cellular oxygen consumption rate (OCR) vs. extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), showed null OCR in cIV-deficient cells (4dKO, 6BKO) and significantly decreased OCR in βKO (cV) cells (Figures 2A and 2C).
evidence.explanation: The 6BKO cells have no measurable oxygen-consumption flux in this assay; the other knockout models in the sentence are distinct genes.

steps/6.description: Patient tissues show reduced or undetectable complex IV activity, with other respiratory complexes preserved in the reported clinical assays. Complete knockout abolishes detectable respiratory flux under the tested HEK293 conditions. This node represents terminal respiratory impairment without asserting universal ATP collapse.

evidence.snippet: We also determined the NAD+/NADH ratio, which was decreased in cIV-deficient cells (4dKO, 6BKO) but was restored to wt levels by AOX expression (Figure 2E).
evidence.explanation: The COX6B1 knockout is 6BKO; AOX bypass reverses reductive imbalance in this cell model.

evidence.snippet: while there was no increase in ROS production in 6BKO (cIV) cells (Figures 4D, 4E, and S4A).
evidence.explanation: The COX6B1-null redox phenotype should not be conflated with increased ROS in the other knockout models.

steps/7.description: The NAD+/NADH ratio falls in COX6B1-null HEK293 cells and normalizes with alternative oxidase expression. Increased mitochondrial ROS and AMPK activation were not observed in this particular knockout model.

evidence.snippet: ECAR in the OXPHOS-deficient cells (4dKO, 6BKO, βKO) indicated a higher glycolytic rate (Figures 2B and 2C), providing ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation.
evidence.explanation: Higher extracellular acidification supports glycolytic compensation in 6BKO, not a measured patient-tissue glycolytic rate.

evidence.snippet: The differences in P-AMPK could not be explained by a drop in ATP levels relative to ADP or AMP, as energy charge remained the same in all cell lines (Figures 4F and S4B).
evidence.explanation: Preserved adenylate energy charge in these cultured knockout cells limits any claim of universal cellular ATP collapse.

steps/8.description: Increased extracellular acidification in COX6B1-null HEK293 cells accompanies preserved adenylate energy charge. This is a culture-dependent compensatory response rather than evidence that ATP is preserved in every affected tissue.

evidence.snippet: The mitochondrial dysfunction was evident in the patient's fibroblasts where defective growth and ATP content were clearly observed in GAL medium as compared with glucose-containing (GLU) medium.
evidence.explanation: ATP depletion is demonstrated under galactose challenge in Arg20Cys fibroblasts; it is not a direct measurement in brain or heart.

evidence.snippet: The differences in P-AMPK could not be explained by a drop in ATP levels relative to ADP or AMP, as energy charge remained the same in all cell lines (Figures 4F and S4B).
evidence.explanation: Preserved adenylate energy charge in these cultured knockout cells limits any claim of universal cellular ATP collapse.

steps/9.description: Arg20Cys patient fibroblasts exhibit low ATP content and poor growth in galactose medium. This conditional assay supports vulnerability when oxidative metabolism is required; preserved energy charge in glucose-supported knockout cells limits a universal ATP-depletion claim.

evidence.snippet: Compared to wt cells, the ATF4 and eIF4EBP1 steady-state levels as well as eIF2α phosphorylation were significantly increased in cIV- (4dKO, 6BKO) and cV- (βKO) deficient models but were normalized by AOX expression only in cIV-deficient cells (4dKO, 6BKO) (Figures 5B and 5C).
evidence.explanation: The 6BKO results establish an integrated stress response that is reversible by respiratory bypass.

evidence.snippet: Despite efficient inhibition of ISR in cIV- (4dKO, 6BKO) and cV- (βKO) lacking cells, documented by (i) a significant decrease of ATF4 and its targets to wt levels (Figures 5E and 5F) and (ii) decreased eIF4EBP1 levels (Figures 5G and 5H), the level of cI subunits was not increased (Figures 5E–5H and S5D–S5F).
evidence.explanation: ISRIB and eIF4EBP1 silencing fail to restore complex I; ISR activation is not established as the mediator of secondary complex I loss.

steps/10.description: COX6B1-null HEK293 cells increase eIF2alpha phosphorylation, ATF4 and eIF4EBP1. Pharmacological or genetic ISR suppression does not restore complex I subunits, so this response is not assigned as their causal mediator.

evidence.snippet: LFQ-MS data analysis of mitochondrial proteins revealed that mitochondrial ribosomal proteins (MRPs), the constituents of both large (mtLSU) and small (mtSSU) mitochondrial ribosome subunits, were in general two to four times decreased in cIV- (4dKO, 6BKO) and cV- (βKO) deficient cells compared to wt (Figures 6A–6C).
evidence.explanation: Proteomics identifies loss of both mitoribosomal subunits in severe COX6B1-null cells.

steps/11.description: Both mitochondrial ribosomal subunits and several assembly factors are reduced in severe COX6B1-null HEK293 cells. The initiating signaling mechanism is unresolved.

evidence.snippet: The synthesis of the mtDNA-encoded cIV and cI subunits was the most affected in cIV- (4dKO, 6BKO) and cV- (βKO) deficient cells, which was reduced to 30% of wt (Figures 7B, 7C, and S6A).
evidence.explanation: Pulse labeling shows reduced mitochondrial synthesis in 6BKO; this is a cellular secondary defect.

steps/6.description: The central cores that define this myopathy histologically represent focal regions of myofibrillar disorganization with depletion of mitochondria and absence of oxidative enzyme activity. Mitochondrial calcium overload from dysfunctional RyR1 channels generates energetic strain and oxidative stress, contributing to the ultrastructural disorganization characteristic of cores.

evidence.snippet: Core elements of treatment include physical therapy, orthopedic interventions, management of respiratory complications, and feeding problems.
evidence.explanation: This review identifies physical therapy as a core management component for core myopathies including central core disease.

treatments/3.description: Regular physical therapy focusing on maintaining range of motion, preventing contractures, and maximizing functional capacity. Exercise programs should be tailored to individual ability.

evidence.snippet: Children should be monitored for the development of scoliosis and other skeletal deformities.
evidence.explanation: This supports active orthopedic monitoring during growth.

evidence.snippet: Congenital dislocation and dysplasia of the hip require orthopedic treatment.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports orthopedic management for hip complications.

treatments/4.description: Surgical and conservative management of musculoskeletal complications including scoliosis, hip dislocation, and foot deformities. Bracing and assistive devices may be needed.

evidence.snippet: Respiratory function should be monitored with serial pulmonary function tests, and where indicated, sleep studies.
evidence.explanation: This supports respiratory surveillance for subclinical or progressive respiratory involvement.

treatments/5.description: Respiratory function should be followed over time, especially in recessive or severe disease and when scoliosis or spinal rigidity is present. Serial pulmonary function testing and sleep studies can detect subclinical nocturnal hypoventilation; respiratory support is managed according to respiratory-muscle involvement.

evidence.snippet: Mutational analysis of the RYR1 gene may provide genetic confirmation of the diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: Supports the role of genetic testing and counseling in CCD diagnosis and family management.

evidence.snippet: It is appropriate to clarify the status of at-risk relatives of an individual diagnosed with MHS to identify those who also have an increased susceptibility to MH and thus would benefit from avoiding anesthetic agents that increase the risk for an MH episode.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports family counseling and risk clarification for malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.

treatments/6.description: Genetic counseling for affected families should discuss autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritance, recurrence risk, variant interpretation, central core disease severity spectrum, and implications for family members regarding malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.

evidence.snippet: Evaluations include: multigene panel testing (if the MHS-related causative variant in the family is known) and muscle biopsy and contracture testing (if the MHS-causative pathogenic variant in the family is not known
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports cascade molecular testing or biopsy/contracture testing depending on whether the familial MHS variant is known.

treatments/7.description: First-degree relatives and other at-risk family members should be offered targeted familial RYR1 variant testing when the pathogenic variant is known. If the molecular cause is unknown or testing is inconclusive, muscle biopsy with contracture testing can clarify MH susceptibility.

evidence.snippet: revealed a disease-specific 5 bp deletion (c.247-10_247-6delCACTC) in a splicing element (pyrimidine tract) of intron 2 adjacent to the third exon of cytochrome c oxidase subunit VIa polypeptide 1 (COX6A1), which is a component of mitochondrial respiratory complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase
evidence.explanation: Gives the founding allele, its splicing mechanism, and the identity of the gene product as a complex IV subunit.

evidence.snippet: Functional analysis showed that expression of COX6A1 in peripheral white blood cells from the affected individuals and COX activity in their EB-virus-transformed lymphoblastoid cell lines were significantly reduced.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates in patient material that the allele reduces both transcript abundance and the enzymatic activity of the complex it belongs to. Graded IN_VITRO rather than HUMAN_CLINICAL because both assays in this sentence are ex vivo - transcript abundance in isolated white blood cells and COX activity in EBV-transformed lymphoblastoid lines - and the human origin of the material is not what evidence_source records.

evidence.snippet: Functional assays demonstrated significantly reduced mutant protein levels (p < 0.01), supporting the pathogenicity of this mutation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the second allelic mechanism as also acting by reducing the amount of COX6A1 protein.

steps/1.description: Two distinct molecular routes to the same endpoint have been reported. The founding allele is a five-base deletion in the polypyrimidine tract of intron 2 (c.247-10_247-6delCACTC) that disrupts splicing of the adjacent third exon; the consequence measured in patients was reduced COX6A1 expression in peripheral white blood cells. The second is a stop-loss substitution that reads through the normal termination codon and extends the protein by 41 residues, reducing steady-state protein levels. Neither is a missense change altering catalysis: both reduce the amount of COX6A1 available, which is why the entry treats the lesion as a dosage problem.

evidence.snippet: COX activity in their EB-virus-transformed lymphoblastoid cell lines were significantly reduced
evidence.explanation: Measures the assembled complex's activity in patient-derived cells, which is the readout of this node.

evidence.snippet: Knockdown of Cox4, Cox5a and Cox6a resulted in reduced CcO activity, diminished affinity of the residual enzyme for oxygen, decreased holoCcO and CcO dimer levels, increased accumulation of CcO subcomplexes and gave rise to an altered pattern of respiratory supercomplexes.
evidence.explanation: Isolates the assembly consequence of losing this specific subunit in human cells: less holoenzyme, accumulated subcomplexes, and disturbed supercomplexes. This is the mechanism that the patient-cell activity measurement above only reports the end result of.

steps/2.description: Reduced COX6A1 leaves the cytochrome c oxidase holoenzyme incompletely assembled. This is the module's trigger node; the disease-specific substitution here is that the lesion is in a structural subunit with a tissue-restricted paralogue, rather than in an assembly factor or metallochaperone shared by all tissues.

evidence.snippet: Respiratory complex IV (CIV, cytochrome c oxidase) is the terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial electron transport chain.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the position of the complex in the chain, from which the consequence of losing it follows. INDIRECT because the paper studies isoform biology in engineered cells, not this disease.

steps/3.description: Less functional cytochrome c oxidase means less electron transfer from reduced cytochrome c to oxygen and less proton pumping, so oxidative ATP synthesis falls. In this disease the deficit is partial rather than complete - patients survive to adulthood in the founding families - which is consistent with a subunit that is reduced rather than absent.

evidence.snippet: The ectopic expression of the heart/muscle-specific isoform of the Cox6 subunit (COX6A2) resulted in restoration of both CcO holoenzyme and activity in COX6A1-knockdown cells.
evidence.explanation: The load-bearing experiment for this node: COX6A2 can functionally replace COX6A1 in human cells depleted of it. INDIRECT because the rescue is engineered in HEK293 cells, so it shows substitution is possible, not that it happens in a patient's muscle.

evidence.snippet: We found extensive CIV-containing supramolecular organization in murine musculature at advanced developmental stages, while a switch in the expression from ubiquitous to muscle-specific isoforms of CIV was also detected.
evidence.explanation: Documents that the isoform switch actually occurs in maturing muscle, which is what makes the rescue experiment above relevant in vivo. INDIRECT: the observation is in normal mouse muscle, and the inference to human nerve versus muscle is the curator's.

evidence.snippet: We also found that the enzymatic activity of CIV containing the muscle-specific isoform COX6A2 was higher than that with COX6A1 in engineered HEK293T cells.
evidence.explanation: Shows the two isoforms are not functionally interchangeable, which is what makes the substitution argument non-trivial rather than a restatement of paralogy.

steps/4.description:
The candidate explanation for why a defect in a housekeeping respiratory subunit presents as a peripheral neuropathy. Adult cardiac and skeletal muscle switch their complex IV 6A subunit from the ubiquitous COX6A1 to the muscle-specific COX6A2, so those high-demand tissues carry a substitute for the missing subunit. Peripheral nerve does not, and long axons have both the highest ATP cost per cell and no capacity for compensatory isoform switching, which would leave them the tissue at risk.
The substitution step is not speculative: forced expression of COX6A2 in COX6A1-knockdown human cells restores both holoenzyme and activity, so the two isoforms are interchangeable at the level of the complex. What is unproven is the step from there to the human disease - nobody has shown that endogenous COX6A2 expression is what protects muscle in a COX6A1-deficient patient, and no CMTRID patient tissue has been compared for COX6A2 content. The node is therefore kept at HYPOTHETICAL: the biochemistry is established, the explanation of the clinical tissue selectivity is not. It is curated rather than omitted because it is the mechanism a reader would otherwise supply silently, and naming it makes it falsifiable.

evidence.snippet: For two consanguineous families with CMT (axonal and mixed phenotypes), a parametric linkage analysis using genome-wide SNP chip identified a 4.3 Mb region on 12q24 showing a maximum multipoint LOD score of 4.23.
evidence.explanation: States the electrophysiological classification of the founding families - axonal in one, mixed in the other - which is the observation behind the intermediate designation.

evidence.snippet: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is a group of hereditary peripheral neuropathies that share clinical characteristics of progressive distal muscle weakness and atrophy, foot deformities, distal sensory loss, as well as diminished tendon reflexes.
evidence.explanation: Gives the shared clinical syndrome this node produces. INDIRECT because the paper is about a different gene; it is cited for the CMT phenotype definition and because its screening panel lists CMTRID/COX6A1 among the recognised recessive CMT genes.

steps/5.description: Length-dependent degeneration of peripheral motor and sensory axons, producing the classic CMT picture of distal weakness, wasting, sensory loss and areflexia. The electrophysiology is what puts this entity in the "intermediate" category: the founding report describes the phenotype as axonal or mixed, meaning conduction velocities that fall between the demyelinating and axonal ranges rather than clearly into one. Curators should note the tension - the entity is named intermediate but the primary description says "axonal or mixed", and both later reports call it axonal.

evidence.snippet: In addition, Cox6a1-null mice showed significantly reduced COX activity and neurogenic muscular atrophy leading to a difficulty in walking.
evidence.explanation: States that the atrophy in the null mouse is neurogenic, which is what distinguishes this node from a primary myopathy.

steps/6.description: Distal muscle wasting secondary to denervation rather than to a primary myopathy. The distinction matters here because the causative gene is a respiratory chain subunit, so a primary mitochondrial myopathy would be the competing explanation; the Cox6a1-null mouse settles it in that model by showing the atrophy is neurogenic.

evidence.snippet: Here we report a 2-year-4-month-old girl who presented with global developmental delay, axonal CMT disease, and elevated lactate levels.
evidence.explanation: Reports the lactate elevation in the one patient in whom it was described.

steps/7.description: Elevated circulating lactate from the shift toward glycolysis when oxidative phosphorylation is limited. This was not a feature of the founding families and appears only in the 2025 case, which is part of why that case raises the question of whether it represents the same entity.

edges/1.description: COX6A1 is a nuclear-encoded structural subunit of the holoenzyme, so less subunit means less assembled complex.

edges/3.description: Which tissues actually experience the energy deficit depends on whether a substitute isoform is available.

edges/5.description: The steps between a chronic partial energy deficit in a neuron and the loss of its distal axon are not established in this disease.

evidence.snippet: Those data indicated that COX6A1 mutation causes the autosomal-recessive axonal or mixed CMT.
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease assertion, made on linkage plus segregation plus functional and mouse data.

evidence.snippet: CMT2S/IGHMBP2, CMT2T/HSJ1, CMTRID/COX6A1, ARAN-NM/HINT and GAN/GAN
evidence.explanation: Independent adoption of the gene-disease pair into a diagnostic screening panel for recessive CMT, which is corroboration of the assertion's acceptance rather than new evidence for it. INDIRECT for that reason.

genes/0.notes: The single causative gene. COX6A1 encodes the ubiquitously expressed 6A subunit of cytochrome c oxidase; the paralogue COX6A2 is muscle-specific and is not known to cause disease. Only two pathogenic alleles have been described - the intron 2 polypyrimidine-tract deletion and a stop-loss substitution - so the allelic spectrum should be read as barely sampled rather than as narrow.

evidence.snippet: Symptomatic management is still the only option, but many therapeutic approaches are under investigation, some in the clinical trial phase.
evidence.explanation: Supports the proposition this entry actually makes - that management is symptomatic. INDIRECT because the review covers Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease as a whole and says nothing about CMTRID.

evidence.snippet: Supportive care, including rehabilitation and orthotics, continues to improve quality of life.
evidence.explanation: Names the specific measures this treatment entry describes. INDIRECT: a group-level review statement, not a CMTRID result.

treatments/0.description: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Management follows general CMT practice - physiotherapy, orthoses and foot surgery for deformity - and no treatment has been reported specifically in CMTRID. This entry deliberately records no drug therapy rather than importing a generic mitochondrial cocktail: no cofactor or antioxidant has been reported to change the course of this disease, and asserting one would be unsupported.

evidence.snippet: Those data indicated that COX6A1 mutation causes the autosomal-recessive axonal or mixed CMT.
evidence.explanation: The recessive inheritance is what the counselling turns on. INDIRECT because the paper establishes the inheritance pattern rather than reporting a counselling intervention.

treatments/1.description: For an autosomal recessive disease with no disease-modifying therapy, reproductive counselling is the one genuinely actionable intervention. Both reported pedigrees were consanguineous or presumed related, which makes cascade carrier testing and the 25 percent sibling recurrence risk the substance of the conversation.

open_questions/0.rationale: The founding families had an adult-compatible peripheral neuropathy and no reported encephalopathy or lactate elevation. The 2025 case had global developmental delay, raised lactate and death after a febrile decompensation at 3.5 years - the natural history of an infantile mitochondrial disease, not of CMT. Two genotypes and three families is not enough to say whether that is allelic severity, a modifier, or a different entity that happens to share a gene. The answer determines whether the developmental and metabolic phenotypes in this entry belong here at all, which is why they are recorded as OCCASIONAL and flagged rather than folded into the core description.

open_questions/1.rationale:
The isoform-substitution evidence is strong but entirely non-human-disease: COX6A2 rescues holoenzyme and activity in COX6A1-knockdown HEK293 cells, and the ubiquitous-to-muscle-specific switch is documented in maturing mouse muscle. What has never been done is the measurement in the disease: no CMTRID patient tissue has been examined for COX6A2 content, and the Cox6a1-null mouse's COX activity was reported without a tissue breakdown. The mismatch is specific rather than general - the model organism that carries the relevant genotype was never asked the question that the cell model was built to answer. Recorded as HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH rather than as a plain knowledge gap because the evidence exists and is good; what is missing is its translation to the human disease.
Note the rescue experiment also constrains what a therapy could look like: if COX6A2 substitutes functionally, inducing it in nerve is a coherent therapeutic hypothesis, and the same paper reports that COX6A2 mRNA did not rise on its own in the knockdown cells - so the substitution would have to be forced rather than coaxed.

open_questions/2.rationale: The disease is catalogued as recessive intermediate D, but the founding paper calls the phenotype axonal or mixed and both subsequent descriptions call it axonal. No paper reports the median motor conduction velocities that the intermediate category is defined by. The label may be a nosological artefact, and a curator matching patients to this entry on the strength of the word "intermediate" could be misled.

evidence.snippet: Autoimmune diseases other than CAD were reported in 8% of patients, cold-induced circulatory symptoms in 91%, and exacerbation of hemolytic anemia during febrile illness in 74%.
evidence.explanation: Cold-induced symptoms in 91% of an unselected national cohort establishes cold exposure as a clinically dominant environmental determinant in this disease.

evidence.snippet: For the first time, we demonstrate fourfold differences between cold and warmer climates regarding prevalence (20 vs 5 cases/million) and incidence (1.9 vs 0.48 cases/million per year).
evidence.explanation: A fourfold difference in prevalence and incidence between cold and warm climates is population-level evidence that ambient temperature shapes who is diagnosed with this disease.

evidence.snippet: Somatic mutations in lysine methyltransferase 2D (KMT2D) and caspase recruitment domain-containing protein 11 (CARD11) encoded proteins were identified in 11 of 16 (69%) and 5 of 16 (31%) patients with CAD, respectively
evidence.explanation: Quantifies how often each somatic lesion is found in CAD patients, establishing them as recurrent rather than anecdotal.

evidence.snippet: The identification of recurrent somatic mutations in the KMT2D and CARD11 genes and trisomies of chromosomes 3, 12, and 18 in a proportion of CAD patients further strengthens the notion of it being a distinct entity
evidence.explanation: Places the somatic mutation profile alongside the recurrent trisomies and ties it to the recognition of CAD-LPD as its own entity.

steps/3.description: The bone-marrow clone that underlies CAD carries recurrent somatic lesions, most consistently loss-of-function mutation of the histone methyltransferase gene KMT2D and gain-of-function mutation of the NF-kB scaffold gene CARD11, together with trisomies of chromosomes 3, 12 and 18. These are somatic events in the neoplastic B cells, not germline predisposition alleles, and their combination is one of the features that separates the CAD clone from lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, in which MYD88 L265P is near-universal and absent here.

evidence.snippet: complement receptor 1 (CR1/CD35) was downregulated 11-fold in clonal CAD B cells compared to control B cells
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the expression difference measured by RNA sequencing of sorted clonal B cells against IgM+ memory B cells from healthy controls.

steps/4.description: RNA sequencing and flow cytometry of sorted clonal CAD B cells show complement receptor 1 (CR1/CD35) to be the most strongly downregulated gene relative to IgM+ memory B cells from healthy donors. CR1 is a negative regulator of B-cell activation and differentiation, so its loss is proposed to lower the activation threshold of the CAD clone and increase its antibody output. The functional consequence is inferred from CR1 biology rather than demonstrated in CAD, so this node is provisional.

evidence.snippet: Bone marrow biopsies showed circumscribed intra-parenchymatous nodules with small monotonous monoclonal B cells in 40/54 patients (median infiltration: 10% of marrow cells) with a CD20(+), IgMs(+), IgDs(+), CD27(+), CD5(-/+), CD11c(-), CD23(-), CD38(-) immunophenotype.
evidence.explanation: The defining histology and immunophenotype of the CAD marrow clone in the 54-patient Nordic pathology series.

evidence.snippet: Of interest, the MYD88 L265P mutation, typical of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, was not detected (17/17 cases).
evidence.explanation: Absence of MYD88 L265P in every tested case is the negative finding that separates this clone from lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma.

evidence.snippet: The 2022 World Health Organization classification formally recognized CAD-associated lymphoproliferative disease as a distinct entity from lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (LPL) and Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM)
evidence.explanation: Records the nosological status of the clone as a WHO-recognised entity, not merely an autoantibody-producing cell population.

evidence.snippet: Primary CAD represents a spectrum of clonal lymphoproliferative bone marrow disorders, in most cases with morphological signs of lymphoma.
evidence.explanation: The population-based Norwegian series reached the same conclusion from 86 unselected patients.

steps/5.description: A small, low-grade clonal B-cell population sits in the bone marrow as circumscribed intraparenchymatous nodules of monotonous CD20+, surface IgM+, IgD+, CD27+, CD23-negative B cells, with a limited number of monotypic IgM+ plasma cells scattered diffusely outside the nodules. It lacks plasmacytoid cytology, the plasma-cell transcription factors MUM1, XBP1 and BLIMP1, and the MYD88 L265P mutation, which is what distinguishes CAD-associated lymphoproliferative disorder from lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma and Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia. The WHO fifth edition recognises it as a distinct entity. This clone is the source of the pathogenic cold agglutinin and the target of B-cell-directed therapy.

evidence.snippet: Primary chronic cold agglutinin disease is a rare hemolytic disease mediated by monoclonal IGHV4-34-encoded cold agglutinins with a predominant specificity for the blood group antigen I.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the IGHV4-34 gene usage and the anti-I specificity of the pathogenic antibody.

evidence.snippet: Monoclonal IgM was detected in 90%; IgG and IgA in 3.5% each; with kappa light chains in 94%.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the isotype and light-chain restriction across an unselected national cohort, supporting "almost always IgM-kappa".

evidence.snippet: All patients had V(H)4-34 encoded IgM kappa cold agglutinins (CA) in high titre.
evidence.explanation: An independent clinical-immunology series in which every patient's cold agglutinin was VH4-34-encoded IgM kappa.

evidence.snippet: Our data also indicate that both CA titre and thermal amplitude are important characteristics when predicting complement activation and clinical course in CAD.
evidence.explanation: Supports the statement that thermal amplitude, not titre alone, governs whether the antibody is pathogenic.

steps/6.description: The secreted paraprotein is a monoclonal IgM, kappa-restricted in about 94% of patients and encoded by IGHV4-34 with somatic hypermutation, whose variable region recognises the carbohydrate blood-group antigen I on the erythrocyte surface. Binding is temperature-dependent: affinity is maximal well below 37 degrees Celsius, and the thermal amplitude — the highest temperature at which the antibody still agglutinates — rather than the titre alone determines whether an individual cold agglutinin is pathogenic in vivo.

evidence.snippet: In CAD, immunoglobulin M (IgM) autoantibodies (cold agglutinins) preferentially bind to the “I” antigen on erythrocytes at temperatures ≤37°C and may result in erythrocyte agglutination.
evidence.explanation: States the temperature dependence of binding and that agglutination is its direct consequence.

evidence.snippet: Most cold agglutinins are immunoglobulin heavy chain (IGH) gene V4‐34 encoded immunoglobulin M kappa (IgMκ), with optimal binding below body temperatures.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that optimal binding occurs below core body temperature, which is what confines agglutination to the acral circulation.

steps/7.description: In the cooler acral circulation — fingers, toes, ears, nose — the monoclonal IgM binds the I antigen and cross-links red cells into agglutinates. This step is purely antibody-mediated and requires no complement: it is the origin of the cold-induced circulatory symptoms, and it is reversible, since the agglutinates disperse as the blood is rewarmed centrally.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, these symptoms are not complement-mediated and are therefore not addressed by complement inhibitors, a distinction with direct therapeutic relevance.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that this branch is independent of the complement chain, which is why it is modelled as a separate limb of the graph.

evidence.snippet: cold-induced circulatory symptoms in 91%
evidence.explanation: Gives the frequency of this branch in an unselected national cohort.

steps/8.description: Agglutinated red cells impede flow through the small vessels of fingers, toes, ears and nose on cold exposure, producing acrocyanosis, Raynaud-like phenomena and livedo reticularis. This branch of the mechanism is purely agglutination-driven: it does not require complement, and complement inhibitors therefore do not relieve it — a distinction with direct therapeutic consequences, since a patient whose dominant complaint is circulatory rather than hemolytic will not benefit from sutimlimab.

evidence.snippet: Autoimmune diseases other than CAD were reported in 8% of patients, cold-induced circulatory symptoms in 91%, and exacerbation of hemolytic anemia during febrile illness in 74%.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that febrile exacerbation is common (74%) and therefore a real feature of the disease, not an anecdote.

steps/9.description: Complement components are acute-phase reactants. During infection or other febrile illness their production rises, restoring the substrate that chronic low-grade consumption had depleted and transiently increasing the hemolytic capacity of an unchanged cold agglutinin. This is the mechanistic explanation for the characteristic paradox that CAD hemolysis worsens during fever rather than improving with the higher body temperature.

evidence.snippet: The immune hemolysis is entirely complement-dependent, predominantly mediated by activation of the classical pathway and phagocytosis of erythrocytes opsonized with complement protein C3b.
evidence.explanation: States that hemolysis in CAD is wholly complement-dependent and runs through the classical pathway, which is the claim of this node.

evidence.snippet: Serum C3 was decreased in nine patients and C4 was decreased in 11 patients, six of whom had reduced CH50. Such data indicate that patients with CAD experience a continuous low-grade complement consumption.
evidence.explanation: Measured C3/C4 depletion is the in-vivo footprint of continuous classical pathway consumption asserted by this node.

steps/10.description: IgM is the most efficient physiological activator of the classical pathway. The surface-bound antigen-IgM complex recruits C1, C1s cleaves C4 and C2, and the assembled C4b2a C3 convertase cleaves C3. Because complement activation proceeds at core temperature once the antibody has bound in the periphery, hemolysis in CAD continues year-round even though the antibody binding step is cold-dependent. Chronic low-grade consumption of C3 and C4 is measurable in the serum of many patients.

evidence.snippet: Diagnosis rests on evidence of hemolysis, a monospecific direct antiglobulin test result positive for C3d but negative for immunoglobulin G (IgG), a cold agglutinin titer ≥ 1:64, and bone marrow evaluation; thermal amplitude can predict clinical severity better than titer alone.
evidence.explanation: The C3d-positive, IgG-negative serological signature is the direct clinical readout of C3b deposition without persistent IgG coating.

steps/11.description: C3b is deposited covalently on the erythrocyte surface. When the cell circulates back to core temperature the IgM dissociates, but the covalently bound C3b does not — which is why the direct antiglobulin test in CAD is strongly positive for C3d (the degradation remnant of C3b) and negative or only weakly positive for IgG. The opsonized cell is now marked for phagocytic clearance and, if the cascade continues, for terminal-pathway lysis.

evidence.snippet: Complete progression to the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) causes intravascular hemolysis, which occurs mainly during acute exacerbations.
evidence.explanation: States both the effect of terminal-pathway completion and its restriction to exacerbations, which is what makes this the minority branch.

evidence.snippet: because of intact CD55- and CD59-mediated regulation in CAD
evidence.explanation: Gives the reason terminal-pathway lysis stays limited in CAD, which is why this node is modelled as a minority branch rather than the main route.

steps/12.description: When C3b density is high enough, C5 convertase forms and the terminal pathway proceeds to the C5b-9 membrane attack complex on the erythrocyte surface. Progression this far is limited in CAD because CD55 and CD59 remain intact on the red cell, unlike in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, so the terminal pathway contributes a minority of hemolysis and does so mainly during acute exacerbations. This is also why C5 inhibition alone gives only a modest hemoglobin response in CAD.

evidence.snippet: Patients were required to have symptomatic disease within 3 months of screening, defined as one or more of the following: symptomatic anemia, acrocyanosis, Raynaud phenomenon, hemoglobinuria, disabling circulatory symptoms, and/or major adverse vascular event, including thrombosis.
evidence.explanation: Hemoglobinuria is one of the recognised disease manifestations used to define symptomatic CAD in a phase 3 trial, which is the clinical signature of the intravascular component.

steps/13.description: Lysis of erythrocytes within the vasculature releases free hemoglobin, which saturates haptoglobin and appears in the urine as hemoglobinuria. In CAD this accounts for a minority of red cell loss and is most evident during cold- or infection-triggered exacerbations.

evidence.snippet: C3b deposition on erythrocytes results in extravascular hemolysis in the liver, the predominant mechanism of erythrocyte destruction in CAD.
evidence.explanation: Identifies hepatic extravascular hemolysis as the predominant destruction mechanism, which is the claim of this node.

evidence.snippet: it explains why therapies effective in warm AIHA, such as corticosteroids and splenectomy, are largely ineffective in CAD, where hemolysis is complement-driven and predominantly hepatic rather than Fc-mediated and splenic
evidence.explanation: Makes the liver-versus-spleen contrast explicit and connects it to the therapeutic consequence recorded in this entry's treatments.

steps/14.description: Kupffer cells, the resident macrophages of the liver sinusoids, express complement receptors that bind C3b-opsonized erythrocytes and phagocytose them. This hepatic, complement-receptor-driven clearance is the dominant mechanism of red cell destruction in CAD, and it is the reason splenectomy fails: unlike warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, where IgG-coated cells are removed by Fc-receptor-bearing splenic red-pulp macrophages, the effector organ here is the liver.

evidence.snippet: Mean baseline hemoglobin level was 9.3 g/dL, but 27% had hemoglobin <8 g/dL.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the severity distribution of the anemia across 232 patients in five countries.

evidence.snippet: At least 51% had received red blood cell transfusions. The mean initial hemoglobin level was 9.2 g/dL (range, 4.5-15.6)
evidence.explanation: Independent population-based confirmation of the hemoglobin level and of how often the anemia becomes transfusion-dependent.

steps/15.description: Destruction of erythrocytes outstrips compensatory erythropoiesis, so hemoglobin falls. Mean hemoglobin at presentation is around 9 g/dL, but a quarter of patients are below 8 g/dL and about half require red-cell transfusion at some point. The anemia is chronic and year-round rather than purely seasonal, because the complement-mediated effector arm operates at core temperature.

evidence.snippet: Risk of TEs was higher in the CAD patient cohort than in the comparison cohort at 1 year (7.2% of CAD patients had TEs vs 1.9% of comparisons)
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the excess thromboembolic risk against a matched general population cohort.

evidence.snippet: Complement-driven endothelial activation is thought to contribute to this prothrombotic state.
evidence.explanation: The proposed mechanism, stated by the source as a belief rather than an established finding, which is why this node is marked hypothetical.

steps/16.description: Patients with CAD have a higher incidence of venous thromboembolism, and of arterial events, than matched controls. Complement-driven endothelial activation is the proposed mediator, but the intermediate steps have not been established in CAD, so this node records an epidemiological association with a hypothesised mechanism rather than a demonstrated causal chain.

evidence.snippet: Mean baseline hemoglobin level was 9.3 g/dL, but 27% had hemoglobin <8 g/dL.
evidence.explanation: Anemia was present in every patient of this 232-patient multinational cohort, with the quoted distribution of severity.

steps/17.description: Chronic anemia of hemolytic type, mean hemoglobin around 9 g/dL, with a substantial minority below 8 g/dL and about half of patients needing transfusion at some point in their course.

evidence.snippet: Clinically meaningful reductions in fatigue were observed by week 1 and were maintained throughout the study.
evidence.explanation: Fatigue was severe enough at baseline in the CARDINAL cohort to permit a clinically meaningful reduction, and it improved within a week of complement blockade.

evidence.snippet: Sutimlimab, but not placebo, significantly increased mean hemoglobin and FACIT-Fatigue scores at treatment assessment timepoint.
evidence.explanation: Confirms in a randomized placebo-controlled setting that fatigue is a measurable, disease-attributable feature rather than a nonspecific complaint.

steps/18.description: Profound fatigue out of proportion to the hemoglobin level, and one of the fastest-responding endpoints to complement inhibition.

evidence.snippet: The most common symptom was acrocyanosis (n = 39 [44%]), and many had symptoms triggered by cold (n = 35 [39%])
evidence.explanation: Gives both the frequency (44% of 89 patients) and the rank of acrocyanosis among presenting symptoms in a single-institution cohort.

steps/19.description: Bluish discoloration of the extremities on cold exposure, caused by agglutinate-induced stasis in the acral microcirculation rather than by hemolysis. It was the single most common presenting symptom in the Mayo Clinic series.

evidence.snippet: Nine patients (40.9%) in the sutimlimab group vs 4 patients (20.0%) in the placebo group had acrocyanosis, and 5 patients (22.7%) vs 3 patients (15.0%), respectively, experienced Raynaud phenomenon.
evidence.explanation: Reports baseline prevalence of Raynaud phenomenon in both arms of a phase 3 CAD cohort, supporting an occasional-frequency assignment.

steps/20.description: Cold-triggered episodic digital pallor, cyanosis and pain. In CADENZA it was present at baseline in 22.7% of the sutimlimab arm and 15.0% of the placebo arm.

evidence.snippet: Cold-induced circulatory symptoms—acrocyanosis of the fingers, toes, ears, and nose, Raynaud-like phenomena, and livedo reticularis—are reported by the great majority of patients (approximately 90%) and can substantially impair daily activities
evidence.explanation: Lists livedo reticularis among the cold-induced circulatory manifestations; the 90% figure covers the group as a whole, not livedo individually, so no frequency is asserted for this phenotype.

steps/21.description: Net-like violaceous mottling of the skin, one of the cold-induced circulatory manifestations of erythrocyte agglutination.

evidence.snippet: The mean bilirubin levels normalized by week 3.
evidence.explanation: Bilirubin was abnormal at baseline across the CARDINAL cohort and normalized on treatment, establishing hyperbilirubinemia as a disease-attributable feature.

steps/22.description: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia from accelerated hemoglobin catabolism. Bilirubin is sensitive enough to hemolytic rate that it normalized within one to three weeks of starting sutimlimab in both pivotal trials.

evidence.snippet: Patients were required to have symptomatic disease within 3 months of screening, defined as one or more of the following: symptomatic anemia, acrocyanosis, Raynaud phenomenon, hemoglobinuria, disabling circulatory symptoms, and/or major adverse vascular event, including thrombosis.
evidence.explanation: Hemoglobinuria is enumerated among the recognised symptomatic manifestations of CAD in the CADENZA eligibility definition.

steps/23.description: Free hemoglobin in the urine, the clinical marker of the intravascular (C5b-9-mediated) component of hemolysis. Typically episodic, during exacerbations.

evidence.snippet: Risk of TEs was higher in the CAD patient cohort than in the comparison cohort at 1 year (7.2% of CAD patients had TEs vs 1.9% of comparisons)
evidence.explanation: Supplies both the presence of the phenotype and the quantitative excess over a matched comparison cohort, which is what the OCCASIONAL band records.

evidence.snippet: CAD seems to be associated with a slightly increased risk of venous thrombosis.
evidence.explanation: Independent multinational cohort reaching the same qualitative conclusion, with the authors' own hedge preserved.

steps/24.description: Excess venous thrombotic events relative to matched controls, reported at 7.2% within one year of diagnosis in a Danish registry cohort.

evidence.snippet: KMT2D and CARD11 genes are recurrently mutated in CAD B cells. KMT2D has loss-of-function mutations, and CARD11 has gain-of-function mutations
evidence.explanation: States the direction of each lesion in the clonal B cells, which is what makes this an oncogenic driver edge rather than a bystander association.
