Cystic hygroma and pulmonary hypoplasia were observed in an ungenotyped fetus from the CCBE1 family, so both individual genetic attribution and a detailed mechanism remain uncertain. Causal edges are withheld. Metopic synostosis and diaphragmatic hernia were isolated CCBE1-positive cohort findings without a demonstrated causal route. Growth hormone deficiency was also named in one cohort case, but the narrative does not supply the testing needed to choose a specific HPO binding; this is retained as a curation lead. Isolated neoplasms and uncertain polydactyly are not generalized into established CCBE1 disease associations.

evidence.snippet: Ultrasound images of hydropic fetus from G4 pregnancy. A, Fetal chest demonstrating pleural effusions; B, fetal head demonstrating scalp edema; C, fetal abdomen demonstrating ascites
evidence.explanation: The confirmed fetus had pleural effusions and ascites; ultrasound establishes their presence rather than the mechanism or composition of the fluid.

evidence.snippet: We report two HS siblings, born to consanguineous parents of Turkish ancestry, whose clinical phenotype also includes protein losing enteropathy, painful relapsing chylous ascites, and hypogammaglobulinemia.
evidence.explanation: The molecularly confirmed siblings establish chylous ascites, but this co-occurrence does not identify the anatomical route of lymph leakage or exclude other contributors.

open_questions/5.rationale: CCBE1-positive patients have pleural effusions and fetal ascites, and other confirmed patients have recurrent chylous ascites. These observations establish the clinical associations but do not resolve the compartment-specific routes of fluid accumulation. Impaired drainage, lymphatic leakage and reduced oncotic pressure may contribute differently. The ultrasound of the confirmed fetus did not characterize the fluid, and the sibling report did not locate a peritoneal leak. These passages do not themselves attribute each effusion to dysplasia as a causal claim, so those arrows are withheld. Unknown intermediates alone would not preclude an indirectly supported causal edge; the missing evidence here is for the compartment-specific causal attribution.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Alcohol and tobacco use; dehydration; physical and emotional stress.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists tobacco among agents to avoid in this disease.

evidence.snippet: Prevention of primary manifestations: Avoid smoking and alcohol abuse.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews prevention guidance names alcohol avoidance.

steps/4.description: Germline gain-of-function variants in PRSS1 (cationic trypsinogen) either enhance autoactivation of trypsinogen to trypsin or destroy the R122 (R117) trypsin-sensitive cleavage site that normally allows prematurely activated trypsin to be inactivated within the pancreas.

steps/5.description: The protease balance shifts toward active trypsin inside the pancreas, because trypsinogen autoactivation is enhanced and the fail-safe inactivation mechanisms (autolysis, SPINK1 inhibition, CTRC-mediated degradation) are outpaced or independently impaired.

steps/6.description: Active trypsin initiates autodigestion of pancreatic acinar tissue and an inflammatory response, the tissue lesion of an acute pancreatitis attack.

evidence.snippet: PRSS1-related hereditary pancreatitis (HP) is characterized by episodes of acute pancreatitis (AP) and recurrent acute pancreatitis (RAP: >1 episode of AP)
evidence.explanation: Reports recurrent acute pancreatitis as the core phenotype.

evidence.snippet: HP was responsible for pancreatic pain (83%), acute pancreatitis (69%)
evidence.explanation: The Rebours national series reports acute pancreatitis in 69% of hereditary pancreatitis patients.

steps/7.description: Recurrent episodes of acute pancreatitis, often beginning in childhood.

evidence.snippet: with frequent progression to chronic pancreatitis (CP)
evidence.explanation: Progression to chronic pancreatitis is characteristic.

evidence.snippet: Manifestations of AP can range from vague abdominal pain lasting one to three days to severe abdominal pain lasting days to weeks and requiring hospitalization.
evidence.explanation: Abdominal pain is the dominant symptom of the acute attacks.

evidence.snippet: HP was responsible for pancreatic pain (83%)
evidence.explanation: Pancreatic pain was the most frequent manifestation (83%) in the Rebours national series.

evidence.snippet: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy to improve digestion in those with pancreatic insufficiency
evidence.explanation: Pancreatic (exocrine) insufficiency is managed with enzyme replacement, evidencing the phenotype.

evidence.snippet: exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (34%, median age of occurrence 29 years)
evidence.explanation: Exocrine insufficiency occurred in 34% of patients at a median age of 29 years in the Rebours national series.

steps/10.description: Exocrine insufficiency with maldigestion as chronic pancreatitis advances.

evidence.snippet: Treatment of glucose intolerance with a regimen typically including metformin and insulin.
evidence.explanation: Endocrine insufficiency (diabetes) is a recognized complication requiring glucose-lowering therapy.

evidence.snippet: diabetes mellitus (26%, median age of occurrence 38 years)
evidence.explanation: Diabetes mellitus occurred in 26% of patients at a median age of 38 years in the Rebours national series.

steps/11.description: Endocrine insufficiency (pancreatogenic/type 3c diabetes) with advancing disease.

evidence.snippet: pancreatic adenocarcinoma (5%, median age 55 years)
evidence.explanation: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma occurred in 5% of patients at a median age of 55 years in the Rebours national series.

evidence.snippet: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is the cause of nearly half the deaths
evidence.explanation: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma accounted for nearly half of deaths in the Rebours national series, underscoring the malignancy risk.

steps/12.description: Markedly increased lifetime risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

evidence.snippet: loss of this cleavage site would permit autodigestion resulting in pancreatitis
evidence.explanation: Conclusion from crystal-structure, molecular-modelling, and protein-digest data that loss of the trypsin-sensitive site permits autodigestion.

edges/2.description: Enhanced autoactivation or loss of the trypsin inactivation site raises active trypsin within the pancreas.

evidence.snippet: providing strong evidence that trypsin plays a central role in premature zymogen activation and pancreatitis
evidence.explanation: Links premature trypsin/zymogen activation to pancreatitis.

edges/3.description: Excess active trypsin triggers the intracellular protease cascade that digests acinar tissue.

edges/4.description: Repeated autodigestive injury produces recurrent acute pancreatitis attacks.

evidence.snippet: with frequent progression to chronic pancreatitis (CP)
evidence.explanation: Recurrent acute injury progresses to chronic pancreatitis.

edges/5.description: Repeated acinar injury drives fibrosis and irreversible chronic pancreatitis.

edges/6.description: Acute pancreatitis attacks present with abdominal pain.

edges/7.description: Recurrent acute attacks progress to chronic pancreatitis.

edges/8.description: Advancing chronic pancreatitis destroys acinar tissue, producing exocrine insufficiency.

edges/9.description: Islet loss in advancing chronic pancreatitis produces pancreatogenic diabetes.

edges/10.description: Chronic pancreatic inflammation markedly raises pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma risk.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Alcohol and tobacco use; dehydration; physical and emotional stress.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews names tobacco as an agent to avoid because it worsens the disease.

edges/11.description: Tobacco use accelerates progression to chronic pancreatitis and raises cancer risk.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: Alcohol and tobacco use; dehydration; physical and emotional stress.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews names alcohol as an agent to avoid.

edges/12.description: Alcohol precipitates and aggravates pancreatitis attacks.

evidence.snippet: an Arg-His substitution at residue 117 of the cationic trypsinogen gene is associated with the HP phenotype
evidence.explanation: Original identification of the causative PRSS1 (cationic trypsinogen) variant.

genes/0.notes: PRSS1 encodes cationic trypsinogen. Gain-of-function variants (most commonly R122H/R117H and N29I/N21I) enhance trypsinogen autoactivation or abolish a trypsin-sensitive inactivation site, increasing intrapancreatic trypsin activity.

evidence.snippet: Mutational screening identified a single A to T mutation resulting in an asparagine to isoleucine transition mutation at position 21 (N21I) in cationic trypsinogen.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the second recurrent PRSS1 variant causing hereditary pancreatitis.

genes/1.notes: The second major PRSS1 variant, N29I (historically N21I), in kindreds lacking R122H.

genes/2.notes: SPINK1 encodes the pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor. Loss-of-function variants (e.g. N34S) reduce trypsin inhibition and raise chronic-pancreatitis risk, typically with recessive/complex inheritance rather than as a classic Mendelian cause.

evidence.snippet: the G191R variant of PRSS2 mitigates intrapancreatic trypsin activity and thereby protects against chronic pancreatitis
evidence.explanation: Establishes PRSS2 G191R as a protective modifier acting on the same trypsin pathway.

genes/3.notes: The anionic trypsinogen G191R variant is degradation-sensitive and protects against chronic pancreatitis.

evidence.snippet: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy to improve digestion in those with pancreatic insufficiency
evidence.explanation: Enzyme replacement is standard for the exocrine insufficiency.

treatments/0.description: Pancreatic enzyme replacement for exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhea, weight loss, micronutrient deficiency).

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Oral pancreatic enzymes substitute for lost exocrine secretion, treating maldigestion.

evidence.snippet: total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation, an irreversible procedure with obligate side effects, in select individuals with severe CP
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes TPIAT as a management option in severe chronic pancreatitis.

treatments/1.description: In selected patients with severe refractory chronic pancreatitis, total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation removes the pain source while preserving beta-cell mass; an irreversible procedure with obligate side effects.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Total pancreatectomy removes the diseased pancreas (the pain source) while islet autotransplantation preserves beta-cell mass.

evidence.snippet: Prevention of primary manifestations: Avoid smoking and alcohol abuse.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews prevention advice centers on smoking and alcohol avoidance.

treatments/2.description: Avoidance of tobacco and alcohol to slow progression and reduce cancer risk.

treatments/3.description: Counseling for autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance and predictive testing of relatives.

evidence.snippet: In vivo synthesis of 1-deoxySa by the mutant enzyme was proportional to the ratio of alanine to serine in the growth media, suggesting that this ratio can be used to modulate the relative synthesis of sphinganine and 1-deoxySa.
evidence.explanation: The dose-response behind the dietary effect, measured in cells: output of the toxic metabolite tracks the alanine-to-serine ratio, which is why an amino acid in the diet can act as a modifier at all.

evidence.snippet: Here we show that the HSAN1 mutations induce a shift in the substrate specificity of SPT, which leads to the formation of the two atypical deoxy-sphingoid bases (DSBs) 1-deoxy-sphinganine and 1-deoxymethyl-sphinganine.
evidence.explanation: The substrate-shift result itself, naming both atypical products, which is the claim this node makes.

evidence.snippet: Surprisingly, the enzymes also had similar affinities for alanine, indicating that the major affect of the C133W mutation is to enhance activation of alanine for condensation with the acyl-CoA substrate.
evidence.explanation: Kinetic evidence that the defect is in activating alanine rather than in binding it or in losing serine affinity, which is the specific basis for the neomorphic grading.

evidence.snippet: Despite earlier reports, canonical activity with l-serine was not reduced in any of the investigated SPT mutants.
evidence.explanation: A uniform isotope-labelling re-assay of eleven SPTLC1 and six SPTLC2 mutants finds canonical serine activity intact, the evidence against reading these variants as loss of function.

evidence.snippet: Simple loss of SPT activity also cannot account for the HSAN1 phenotype, since heterozygous SPTLC1 knock-out mice have reduced SPT activity but are otherwise normal.
evidence.explanation: The in vivo counterpart of the same argument: halving SPT activity in mice produces no neuropathy, so reduced activity is not the pathogenic step.

steps/2.description: Serine palmitoyltransferase catalyses the condensation of palmitoyl-CoA with L-serine, the first and rate-limiting step of de novo sphingolipid synthesis. HSAN1A variants in the SPTLC1 subunit enhance the enzyme's activation of L-alanine and of glycine as alternative substrates, so the mutant enzyme makes products the wild-type enzyme makes only in trace amounts. Kinetic work on C133W found wild-type and mutant enzymes to have similar affinities for both serine and alanine, locating the defect in activation of alanine rather than in substrate binding, which is why the variant is curated as neomorphic rather than as a loss of function.

evidence.snippet: Both metabolites lack the C(1) hydroxyl group of sphinganine and can therefore neither be converted to complex sphingolipids nor degraded.
evidence.explanation: The chemical reason the products accumulate instead of being metabolised, which is what this node asserts.

evidence.snippet: Elevated DSB levels were also found in the plasma of HSAN1 patients and confirmed in three groups of HSAN1 patients with different SPTLC1 mutations.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the accumulation in patients rather than only in transfected cells, across three SPTLC1 genotypes.

evidence.snippet: are associated with increased levels of the deoxysphingoid bases 1-deoxy-sphinganine and 1-deoxymethyl-sphinganine in patients' plasma samples
evidence.explanation: Extends the plasma elevation to two further SPTLC1 alleles. The quote is trimmed to the plasma clause: the full sentence also reports reduced SPT activity in vitro, which is a different kind of evidence and is contested by the later uniform re-assay, so quoting it whole would grade an in vitro result as HUMAN_CLINICAL. The activity claim is curated separately on the substrate-shift node and in the attached discussion.

steps/3.description: 1-deoxysphinganine and 1-deoxymethylsphinganine lack the C1 hydroxyl group of a canonical sphingoid base. That hydroxyl is required both for conversion into complex sphingolipids and for entry into the normal degradation route, so these metabolites accumulate rather than turning over. They are elevated in the plasma of patients carrying several different SPTLC1 alleles, which makes this node the disease's accessible biomarker as well as its mechanism.

evidence.snippet: we show that exogenous application of these deoxysphingoid bases causes dose- and time-dependent neurotoxicity in primary mammalian neurons, as determined by analysis of cell survival and neurite length
evidence.explanation: The dose-response demonstration that the accumulated metabolites kill neurons, in both motor and sensory primary cultures.

evidence.snippet: The changes in intracellular Ca2+ handling are accompanied by an early loss of mitochondrial membrane potential in deoxysphingoid base-treated motor and sensory neurons.
evidence.explanation: Names the proximate subcellular mechanism this node asserts.

evidence.snippet: The neurotoxicity co-occurs with a disturbed neurofilament structure in neurites when cultured in the presence of DSBs.
evidence.explanation: A second, independent cellular correlate of the toxicity, in the paper that first identified the metabolites.

evidence.snippet: Notably, blocking NMDAR activation by MK-801 or memantine significantly prevented 1-deoxySA neurotoxicity.
evidence.explanation: A pharmacological test of the toxicity's route: blocking NMDA receptors prevents it, which implicates glutamate-receptor signalling alongside the calcium and mitochondrial changes.

evidence.snippet: HSN1 iPSC-derived sensory neurons (iPSCdSNs) endogenously produce neurotoxic DSBs.
evidence.explanation: Moves the claim from exogenous application to endogenous production: patient-derived sensory neurons make the metabolites themselves, so the toxicity is not an artefact of adding lipid to the medium.

evidence.snippet: Complex gangliosides, which are essential for membrane micro-domains and signaling, are reduced, and neurotrophin signaling is impaired, resulting in reduced neurite outgrowth.
evidence.explanation: Names a further consequence in patient-derived neurons: the sphingolipid products the cell should be making are depleted downstream, not only the atypical ones added.

steps/4.description: Deoxysphingoid bases are toxic to primary sensory and motor neurons in a dose- and time-dependent way, with disturbed endoplasmic-reticulum and mitochondrial calcium handling and early loss of mitochondrial membrane potential as proximate cellular effects, and with disturbed neurofilament structure in neurites. Degeneration is length-dependent, so the longest axons in the lower limbs fail first, which is why the clinical picture begins in the feet and why epidermal innervation is lost at the distal leg before the thigh.

evidence.snippet: Reduction of serine levels in mice led to increases in levels of retinal deoxysphingolipids and compromised visual function.
evidence.explanation: Shows that raising retinal deoxysphingolipids is sufficient to impair vision in an animal, which is the mechanism this node asserts.

evidence.snippet: Elevated levels of atypical deoxysphingolipids, caused by variant SPTLC1 or SPTLC2 or by low serine levels, were risk factors for macular telangiectasia type 2, as well as for peripheral neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: The authors' conclusion tying the same metabolite to both the retinal and the peripheral-nerve phenotype.

steps/5.description: Deoxysphingolipids also affect the macula. Lowering serine in mice raised retinal deoxysphingolipid levels and compromised visual function, and the metabolites killed photoreceptors in human retinal organoids. Most HSAN1 patients examined ophthalmologically have macular telangiectasia type 2, which is otherwise an orphan disease, so the ocular phenotype is part of the SPT substrate-shift syndrome rather than a coincidence.

evidence.snippet: The first symptoms were universally sensory and occurred at a median age of 20 years (range 14-54 years).
evidence.explanation: Sensory symptoms were universal and first in 23 genotyped patients, which is the basis for the OBLIGATE frequency and for the onset figure.

evidence.snippet: Among those with sensory loss, all described a stocking-glove distribution, and more reported impaired temperature perception than light touch or pressure.
evidence.explanation: Records the distribution and the small-fibre predominance.

steps/6.description: Length-dependent distal sensory loss in a stocking-glove distribution, beginning in the feet and spreading proximally, with the hands involved on average a decade later. It is the presenting feature in every reported cohort.

evidence.snippet: Loss of pain sensation leads to chronic skin ulcers and distal amputations.
evidence.explanation: States the loss of pain sensation and its consequence in the paper reporting the founding SPTLC1 families. The sentence introduces the disease rather than reporting this study's own measurement.

steps/7.description: Loss of nociception, predominating over light touch and pressure. This is the deficit that makes the injuries painless.

evidence.snippet: Among those with sensory loss, all described a stocking-glove distribution, and more reported impaired temperature perception than light touch or pressure.
evidence.explanation: Records the thermal deficit and that it predominates over the large-fibre modalities in this cohort.

steps/8.description: Loss of thermal perception, reported more often than impaired light touch or pressure in the natural-history cohort. It is the reason GeneReviews asks patients to be taught burn prevention.

evidence.snippet: prominent early sensory loss and later positive sensory phenomena including dysesthesia and characteristic "lightning" or "shooting" pains
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews characterisation of the pain and of its timing relative to the sensory loss.

evidence.snippet: With regard to painful symptoms, 10 of 23 (43%) patients reported tingling, and 5 of 23 (22%) reported burning.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the character of the pain in the 23-patient cohort. The OBLIGATE band rests on the same cohort's symptom table, which records shooting pain in 23 of 23; that table row cannot be quoted as a snippet because the cached row carries colspan markers in square brackets and the validator strips bracketed spans from the snippet but not from the source, so no exact substring spans the row.

evidence.snippet: Two patients reported that gabapentin and venlafaxine improved their symptoms significantly, but many patients reported that their pain was refractory to all medications.
evidence.explanation: Records how poorly the pain responds to treatment, which is why it dominates quality of life in this disease.

steps/9.description: Positive sensory phenomena appearing later than the sensory loss: dysesthesia and the characteristic lightning or shooting pains, reported by every patient in the natural-history cohort and often refractory to medication.

evidence.snippet: Electrophysiological studies revealed inability to elicit any sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) in the arms or legs in 5 of 8 patients.
evidence.explanation: The electrophysiological measurement behind this phenotype.

evidence.snippet: In aggregate, nerve conduction studies confirmed the presence of significant large-fiber involvement of both sensory and motor fibers.
evidence.explanation: The authors' summary, which is also the evidence that large fibres are involved alongside the small-fibre deficit seen on skin biopsy.

steps/10.description: Nerve conduction studies show absent or markedly reduced sensory nerve action potentials with preserved conduction velocities where responses remain, the electrophysiological signature of an axonal rather than demyelinating process. Compound muscle action potentials are also lost in most patients.

evidence.snippet: Skin biopsies revealed universally absent epidermal innervation at the distal leg with relative preservation in the thigh.
evidence.explanation: The biopsy finding and its length-dependent gradient.

evidence.snippet: These results confirm sensory loss as the initial symptom of HSAN1 and suggest that skin biopsy may be the most promising biomarker for future clinical trials.
evidence.explanation: Why this finding is curated as diagnostic rather than as a bare histological observation.

steps/11.description: Epidermal innervation is absent at the distal leg in adults while some remains at the thigh, and thigh density correlates with clinical severity and with motor amplitudes. This is the most promising biomarker identified for trials in this disease.

evidence.snippet: Motor involvement is present in all advanced cases and can be severe.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews statement that motor involvement is a core feature of advanced disease, not an occasional add-on.

evidence.snippet: Foot weakness came first, with hand weakness following, on average, 7.6 years later
evidence.explanation: The sequence and interval within the motor deficit. The cohort's symptom table records weakness in 21 of 23 patients, which is the basis for the VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/12.description: Weakness of the feet, later the hands, beginning on average some years after the sensory deficit. It affected 21 of 23 patients in the natural-history cohort and may become severe enough to require walking aids or, in advanced disease, a wheelchair.

evidence.snippet: After age 20 years, the distal wasting and weakness may involve proximal muscles, possibly leading to wheelchair dependency by the seventh or eighth decade.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews description of the wasting and of its later proximal spread.

steps/13.description: Wasting of distal limb muscles following denervation, progressing after age 20 years to involve more proximal muscles in some patients.

evidence.snippet: Loss of sensation can lead to painless injuries, which, if unrecognized, result in slow wound healing and subsequent osteomyelitis requiring distal amputations.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews account of the chain from sensory loss through painless injury to amputation, which is the chain this entry models as sequelae.

steps/14.description: Unrecognised injuries, burns and pressure lesions of insensate extremities. Because they are not felt, they are not protected, and they heal slowly.

evidence.snippet: Seventeen of 23 patients (74%) reported ulcers.
evidence.explanation: The measured proportion in a genotyped cohort, which is the basis for the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: The ulcers were restricted to the lower extremities in 17 patients and affected both the upper and lower extremities in 4 patients.
evidence.explanation: Records the distribution of the ulceration.

steps/15.description: Chronic, poorly healing ulcers of the distal extremities, overwhelmingly of the feet. They developed in 17 of 23 patients in the natural-history cohort at a mean of 8.1 years after the first neuropathic symptom, and they are the complication that dominates long-term morbidity.

evidence.snippet: result in slow wound healing and subsequent osteomyelitis requiring distal amputations
evidence.explanation: Names osteomyelitis as the step between the non-healing wound and amputation.

steps/16.description: Infection of bone beneath chronic neuropathic ulcers. It is the usual indication for the distal amputations that roughly a third of patients undergo.

evidence.snippet: Approximately one-third of patients required distal limb amputations.
evidence.explanation: The measured proportion, which is the basis for the FREQUENT band and for treating amputation as an expected outcome rather than a rare one.

steps/17.description: Amputation of toes, feet or fingers for uncontrolled infection of insensate extremities. About one third of patients in the natural-history cohort had undergone one.

evidence.snippet: ankle/foot orthotics for foot drop; arthrodesis for Charcot joints
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews records Charcot joints among the manifestations requiring management, which is the evidence that they occur in this disease.

steps/18.description: Charcot joint destruction from repeated unperceived trauma to insensate joints, managed surgically by arthrodesis.

evidence.snippet: Two variants known to cause HSAN1 were identified as causal for macular telangiectasia type 2: of 11 patients with HSAN1, 9 also had macular telangiectasia type 2.
evidence.explanation: The proportion of HSAN1 patients found to have the retinal phenotype. The abstract's 9 of 11 is 9 of 13 in the results text, once two further families are counted, and the entry bands the phenotype on the larger denominator the results text gives: 9 of 13 is 69%, which is FREQUENT rather than VERY_FREQUENT. Either way the band rests on one small series examined because the link was already suspected.

evidence.snippet: Macular telangiectasia type 2 is an orphan disease, affecting approximately 1 in 5000 persons.
evidence.explanation: The background rate that makes the co-occurrence a disease feature rather than chance.

steps/19.description: Macular telangiectasia type 2, with parafoveal capillary abnormality and macular thinning, found in 9 of 13 HSAN1 patients examined in the one study that looked for it. Since it affects roughly 1 in 5000 people in general, it is part of this disease rather than a coincidence, and it is the reason to examine the retina in a patient with an SPT variant.

evidence.snippet: Consequently, they accumulate in the cell, as demonstrated in HEK293 cells overexpressing mutant SPTLC1 and lymphoblasts of HSAN1 patients.
evidence.explanation: Links the enzymatic shift to accumulation of the products, in cells expressing the mutant subunit and in patient lymphoblasts.

edges/1.description: Condensation of palmitoyl-CoA with L-alanine yields 1-deoxysphinganine and with glycine yields 1-deoxymethylsphinganine.

evidence.snippet: The DSBs show pronounced neurotoxic effects on neurite formation in cultured sensory neurons.
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration that the metabolites harm sensory neurons, which is the causal claim this edge makes.

edges/2.description: The accumulated deoxysphingoid bases are directly toxic to cultured sensory and motor neurons.

evidence.snippet: Deoxysphingolipids caused photoreceptor-cell death in retinal organoids, but not in the presence of regulators of lipid metabolism.
evidence.explanation: Shows the accumulated metabolites are toxic in retinal tissue as well as in peripheral neurons, which is the link to the ocular phenotype.

edges/3.description: The same metabolites reach the retina, where they cause photoreceptor death in human retinal organoids.

evidence.snippet: Sensory problems were universal and appeared first.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the sensory deficit is the first and universal clinical consequence in a genotyped HSAN1 cohort.

edges/4.description: Degeneration of the longest sensory axons produces the length-dependent distal sensory deficit that opens the clinical picture.

edges/5.description: Small-fibre loss removes protective nociception.

edges/6.description: The same small-fibre loss removes thermal perception, which is what makes unnoticed burns possible.

edges/7.description: Degenerating sensory neurons also generate positive sensory phenomena, the characteristic shooting or lancinating pains.

evidence.snippet: None of the 6 patients who underwent skin biopsies of the distal leg and thigh had any epidermal innervation remaining at the distal leg site, whereas some epidermal innervation always remained at the thigh site, consistent with the known length-dependent pattern of the neuropathy
evidence.explanation: The skin-biopsy measurement, and the distal-versus-thigh gradient that makes it length-dependent degeneration rather than a global deficit.

edges/8.description: Loss of the distal-most sensory terminals, measurable on skin biopsy, is the histological correlate of the small-fibre deficit.

edges/9.description: Loss of large myelinated sensory fibres is what abolishes sensory nerve action potentials on nerve conduction studies.

evidence.snippet: Motor axonopathy was severe as assessed by symptoms, signs, and electrophysiological study, whereas autonomic neuropathy was scant.
evidence.explanation: The authors' summary of their own cohort data, which is the basis for modelling motor involvement as a core consequence rather than a rarity.

edges/10.description: Motor axons degenerate as well, which is why weakness follows the sensory deficit in most patients despite the disease's name.

edges/11.description: Denervation of distal limb muscles produces wasting.

edges/12.description: Retinal deoxysphingolipid toxicity is the proposed basis of the macular telangiectasia type 2 seen in most examined HSAN1 patients.

edges/13.description: Sensory loss removes the warning that would prevent injury to the feet and hands.

edges/14.description: Unperceived trauma to insensate extremities.

edges/15.description: Unperceived burns to insensate extremities.

edges/16.description: Unprotected injuries on insensate feet break down into chronic ulcers.

edges/17.description: Repeated unperceived trauma to insensate joints destroys them.

edges/18.description: Chronic ulcers become infected and the infection reaches bone.

edges/19.description: Osteomyelitis that cannot be controlled is treated by amputation.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, a 10% L-alanine–enriched diet increased dSL levels and led to severe peripheral neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: The alanine arm in the C133W mouse raises both the metabolite and the severity of the neuropathy, which is the specific claim this link makes.

edges/20.description: Raising alanine relative to serine gives the mutant enzyme more of the substrate it wrongly prefers, increasing 1-deoxysphingolipid formation.

evidence.snippet: We found two mutations to be located in exon 5 (C133Y and C133W) and one mutation to be located in exon 6 of SPTLC1 (V144D).
evidence.explanation: Names the founding causative SPTLC1 alleles and their exons.

evidence.snippet: We report here that the gene encoding a subunit of serine palmitoyltransferase is located within the HSN1 locus, expressed in dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and mutated in HSN1.
evidence.explanation: Independent simultaneous identification of SPTLC1 as the HSN1 gene, noting its expression in the dorsal root ganglia that degenerate in this disease.

evidence.snippet: This indicates that the G387A mutation is most likely not directly associated with HSAN I.
evidence.explanation: Removes G387A from the causative allele set, so the gene-disease claim rests on the functionally confirmed variants rather than on all four originally reported ones.

evidence.snippet: In accordance with previous reports, a mutation in Ser331 in the present patient was associated with early-onset and a severe phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Records the Ser331 genotype-phenotype correlation within SPTLC1.

evidence.snippet: Our report adds to the growing evidence of the existence of an overlap between hereditary neuropathy and motor neuron disease caused by pathogenic p.S331Y variant in SPTLC1 gene.
evidence.explanation: Evidence that Ser331 sits on the boundary between this disease and the SPTLC1 motor neuron disease: the same variant is reported with features of both, which is why the entry describes an overlap rather than a clean split by variant position.

evidence.snippet: The p.Cys133Trp mutation in SPTLC1 is the most common cause of HSAN in the UK population and should be screened first in all patients with sporadic or autosomal dominant HSAN.
evidence.explanation: Gives SPTLC1 C133W its place in the genetic differential: in a 140-patient UK cohort screened across six HSAN genes, it was the single commonest cause, which is why it is sequenced first there.

evidence.snippet: The Australian and English families may therefore have a common founder who, on the basis of historical information, has been determined to have lived in southern England prior to 1800.
evidence.explanation: Haplotype evidence that the recurrent C133W allele is a founder mutation rather than a recurrent mutation hotspot, which is why it dominates British and Australian series in particular.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous missense variants. The founding alleles C133Y, C133W and V144D lie in exons 5 and 6, and C133Y and C133W are the recurrent founder alleles. Variants at Ser331 cause an early-onset severe form with prominent weakness. The originally reported G387A variant was later shown not to be disease associated. SPTLC1 variants that instead cause excess canonical sphingolipid synthesis produce a different disease, juvenile ALS27, which is curated separately as Amyotrophic_Lateral_Sclerosis_27_Juvenile.

evidence.snippet: CONCLUSION: High-dose oral l-serine supplementation appears safe in patients with HSAN1 and is potentially effective at slowing disease progression.
evidence.explanation: The trial's own conclusion, stated with the hedge the authors used. The trial enrolled 18 participants, so this is a small Class I result rather than a definitive one.

evidence.snippet: After 1 year, the l-serine group experienced improvement in CMTNS relative to the placebo group
evidence.explanation: The clinical outcome, which is what separates this from the earlier metabolite-only evidence.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, a 10% L-alanine–enriched diet increased dSL levels and led to severe peripheral neuropathy.

treatments/4.description: Preclinical only. Because the disease is caused by a product the mutant allele makes rather than by loss of the normal one, silencing the mutant transcript and leaving the wild-type allele intact is mechanistically the right target. GalNAc-conjugated locked-nucleic-acid gapmer antisense oligonucleotides against the p.S331F allele achieved over 90% mutant transcript silencing in liver and dorsal root ganglia of S331F mice, lowered blood 1-deoxysphingoid bases and reversed the aberrant dorsal-root-ganglion gene expression. No human study has been performed, and the construct is allele specific, so it would have to be remade for each variant.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Removing the mutant transcript removes the enzyme subunit that makes the atypical products, which lowers the metabolite itself rather than competing with it.

open_questions/0.rationale: Early work reported reduced SPT activity for C133W, C133Y and V144D, and the first transgenic mouse paper was titled on dominant inhibition of the enzyme. A later uniform isotope-labelling re-assay of eleven SPTLC1 and six SPTLC2 mutants found canonical serine activity was not reduced in any of them, and that the Ser331 variants, which cause the most severe disease, showed increased canonical activity. The two accounts are not reconciled in the literature. The difference is not cosmetic: it decides whether this is a neomorphic or a loss-of-function disease, and therefore whether substrate competition alone is the right therapeutic principle. This entry follows the later uniform re-assay, supported by the mouse genetics, in which halving SPT activity produces no neuropathy and excess wild-type subunit rescues the mutant phenotype.

open_questions/1.rationale: The randomised trial enrolled 18 participants and 16 completed it, so a 1.5-unit CMTNS difference at one year is a real but small result in a disease measured in decades. Two questions follow. First, the natural history places the first symptoms at a median age of 20 with subtle symptoms years earlier, and the authors of that study argue the optimal window for intervention is childhood, which no trial has tested. Second, intraepidermal nerve fibre density at the thigh is the biomarker proposed for future trials, and it was a secondary outcome here rather than a demonstrated responder. Whether the treatment arrests, slows or merely delays the degeneration is not settled by the existing data.

open_questions/2.rationale: The single study that examined HSAN1 patients ophthalmologically found the retinal phenotype in 9 of 13, against a population rate near 1 in 5000, so the association is not in doubt. The rate is another matter: the series is small, the patients were examined because the link was suspected, and the four without a definite diagnosis were all under 50 and taking serine supplements, which the authors suggest may delay onset. That last point makes the frequency and the treatment question the same question, and neither has been addressed prospectively.

Ascertainment is by electronic medical record within a hospital biorepository, and the study reports no enzyme activity values.

hypotheses/0.description: Mucopolysaccharidosis type I — Hurler syndrome (severe), Hurler-Scheie (intermediate), and Scheie (attenuated) — is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in IDUA encoding α-L-iduronidase. Loss of α-L-iduronidase activity prevents lysosomal degradation of heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate, producing pathological GAG accumulation in lysosomes of multiple cell types. Substrate storage drives progressive coarsening, dysostosis multiplex, hepatosplenomegaly, cardiac valvular and myocardial disease, corneal clouding, recurrent airway obstruction, and (in severe Hurler) progressive neurodevelopmental regression. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (the standard of care for severe Hurler before age 2), enzyme replacement therapy (laronidase), and emerging gene therapy approaches corroborate the IDUA-deficiency / GAG-accumulation axis as the canonical pathogenic mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Ascending aortic diameters were significantly greater, left ventricular function significantly decreased, and AI significantly more frequent in B6 MPSI mice compared to NSG MPSI mice (p < 0.0001, p = 0.008 and p = 0.02, respectively); NSG and B6 WT mice showed no changes.
evidence.explanation: The cardiac phenotype separates immunocompetent from immunodeficient MPS I mice, which is the observation that makes translation to human disease the open question recorded here.

evidence.snippet: These results suggest that the innate and adaptive immune systems play a role in these cardiac findings which may be relevant to human MPSI.
evidence.explanation: The authors state human relevance as a suggestion rather than a demonstrated result, which is precisely the mismatch this discussion records.

open_questions/0.rationale: Immunocompetent C57BL/6 MPS I mice develop ascending aortic dilation, aortic insufficiency and reduced left ventricular function, while immunodeficient NSG MPS I mice with the same degree of urinary glycosaminoglycan elevation do not. The immunocompetent aortas upregulated all eleven components of the inflammasome pathway and carried medial macrophage and adventitial T-cell infiltrates that the immunodeficient aortas lacked. If that dependency holds in people, glycosaminoglycan storage is not by itself sufficient for the cardiac phenotype, and anti-inflammatory adjunctive therapy becomes a plausible addition to enzyme restoration. Three things keep this out of the causal graph. The study is small, with 12 immunocompetent and 8 immunodeficient mutant male mice, and its authors describe it as a preliminary study. Tissue glycosaminoglycan was never quantified, only urinary excretion, so equivalent storage in the aortic wall is assumed rather than shown. The two strains differ in genetic background as well as in immune competence. No human study has tested immune suppression or inflammasome blockade for MPS I cardiovascular disease.

evidence.snippet: Despite HSCT, considerable residual disease burden and ensuing corrective surgical interventions were observed in all, and at every decade of follow-up post HSCT.
evidence.explanation: Three decades of follow-up in 25 successfully transplanted Hurler patients establish the observation this gap is about: enzyme restoration that is sufficient to change the natural history does not stop somatic disease accruing.

open_questions/1.rationale: Transplantation restores donor-derived alpha-L-iduronidase, and a normal post-transplant enzyme level predicts superior long-term outcomes across organ systems. Yet residual burden requiring corrective surgery is observed in all patients at every decade of follow-up, and restrictive lung disease is present in every treated patient able to complete testing. Two explanations fit these data and have not been separated. Damage may accrue irreversibly before transplantation, which is typically performed near two years of age, and circulating enzyme may reach avascular cartilage, bone, heart valve and cornea poorly, which is what the enzyme replacement literature already reports. Alternatively, secondary cascades downstream of storage may become self-sustaining and stop responding to substrate clearance. Which is right determines whether the remedy is earlier or better enzyme delivery, or a second agent aimed at a downstream cascade. Serial multi-omic sampling from before transplantation through several years afterwards, and conditional restoration of Idua at different disease stages in animals, would separate them.

evidence.snippet: Recognizing distinct eosinophil subsets is crucial for understanding their contributions to disease progression. This review highlights recent discoveries in eosinophil diversity and explores therapeutic implications of selectively targeting specific eosinophil subsets in clinical practice.
evidence.explanation: This review identifies eosinophil diversity as relevant to disease progression and subset-selective therapeutic strategies.

evidence.snippet: Specifically, resident eosinophils (rEos) reside in tissues for local maintenance and immune regulation, whereas inflammatory eosinophils (iEos) are rapidly recruited during immune responses to drive inflammation.

evidence.snippet: The proteolytic actions induced by eosinophil granules may activate the kallikrein system and so the clotting cascade by factor XII activation; the factor XII activation, increasing the activation of other proteases of clotting system, induces hypercoagulable state.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, the eosinophil activation and degranulation increases the release of eosinophil cationic protein that is able to bind heparin and modulate thrombomodulin so reducing the physiological anticoagulation mechanisms and so increasing the prothrombotic state in hypereosinophilia.
evidence.explanation: Supports a second, anticoagulation-impairing mechanism by which activated eosinophils promote thrombosis.

This thromboinflammatory branch is clinically important because thrombosis is a frequent complication and can dominate long-term morbidity.

evidence.snippet: Mepolizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody. In conditions where eosinophilia is considered to play an important part in the pathology, including eosinophilic asthma, HES, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a consistent reduction in blood eosinophil counts is observed in association with mepolizumab administration, with concomitant clinical improvement.
evidence.explanation: Trial registration directly supports targeted anti-IL-5 therapy in severe HES.

evidence.snippet: This is a multicentre, randomised, double-blind (DB), parallel-group, placebo-controlled, 24-week Phase III study to compare the efficacy and safety of benralizumab versus placebo administered by SC injection Q4W in patients with hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES).
evidence.explanation: Supports ongoing phase III evaluation of anti-IL-5R therapy in HES.

treatments/2.description: Targeted monoclonal antibodies against the IL-5 axis are used for severe or relapsing disease and are especially relevant when eosinophilia remains corticosteroid-dependent or corticosteroid-refractory.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: These agents reduce eosinophil burden by interrupting IL-5 pathway signaling.

evidence.snippet: Cellular transfection studies showed that the two mutations resulted in local accumulations of nexilin and that the expressed fragment of actin-binding domain containing p.Q131E completely lost the ability to bind F-actin in C2C12 cells.
evidence.explanation: Direct in vitro demonstration that the p.Q131E variant abolishes F-actin binding by the nexilin actin-binding domain, establishing the proposed molecular lesion.

evidence.snippet: Coimmunoprecipitation assay indicated that the p.Q131E mutation decreased the binding of full-length NEXN to α-actin and abolished the interaction between the fragment of actin-binding domain and α-actin.
evidence.explanation: Independent biochemical confirmation that the variant disrupts the nexilin-actin interaction in the context of the full-length protein.

steps/1.description: Nexilin (NEXN) is an F-actin-binding protein of the cardiac Z-disc, not a component of the thick or thin filament. The two HCM-reported missense variants lie in or adjacent to the actin-binding domain: in transfected C2C12 cells they caused abnormal local accumulation of nexilin, and the actin-binding-domain fragment carrying p.Q131E lost F-actin binding entirely, with coimmunoprecipitation showing reduced binding of full-length NEXN to alpha-actin. The proposed proximal lesion is therefore failure of the nexilin-actin anchorage that couples thin filaments to the Z-disc, rather than an alteration of cross-bridge cycling. Confidence is PROVISIONAL: the functional data are robust in vitro but derive from the same single report that proposed the gene-disease association, which has since been classified Limited by ClinGen.

evidence.snippet: Nexilin, encoded by NEXN, is a cardiac Z-disc protein recently identified as a crucial protein that functions to protect cardiac Z-discs from forces generated within the sarcomere.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the load-bearing, Z-disc-protective role of nexilin that the proposed mechanism depends on.

evidence.snippet: Increasing mechanical strain aggravated Z-disk damage in nexilin-deficient skeletal muscle, implying a unique role of nexilin in protecting Z-disks from mechanical trauma.
evidence.explanation: Supports load-dependent Z-disc failure as the consequence of nexilin loss, but only PARTIAL for CMH20 — this study characterizes nexilin loss in zebrafish and in human DILATED cardiomyopathy, and the resulting phenotype was dilated rather than hypertrophic.

steps/2.description: The Z-disc is the mechanical integration site that anchors myofilaments and transmits contractile force between adjacent sarcomeres. Nexilin was identified as a Z-disc protein whose specific role is to protect the Z-disc from the forces generated within the sarcomere; loss-of-function models show that Z-disc damage in nexilin-deficient muscle is aggravated by increasing mechanical strain. The inferred consequence of impaired nexilin-actin anchorage is therefore progressive Z-disc destabilization under contractile load. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: the direct experimental evidence for this step comes from nexilin-deficient zebrafish and from human DILATED cardiomyopathy carriers, not from the HCM families — in those models Z-disc failure produced a dilated, not hypertrophic, phenotype. The step is retained as HYPOTHETICAL for CMH20 because no HCM-specific model system has been reported.

evidence.snippet: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), the most common inherited cardiac disorder, is characterized by increased ventricular wall thickness that cannot be explained by underlying conditions, cadiomyocyte hypertrophy and disarray, and increased myocardial fibrosis.
evidence.explanation: Defines the hypertrophic remodeling endpoint. PARTIAL because this is the paper's general description of HCM as a disease class, not a report of myocardial histopathology in the NEXN variant carriers themselves. (The quoted text reproduces the source's typographic error "cadiomyocyte".)

steps/3.description: The tissue-level endpoint that defines the hypertrophic phenotype: cardiomyocyte hypertrophy with myofibrillar/sarcomeric disarray and increased interstitial myocardial fibrosis, producing ventricular wall thickening that is not explained by loading conditions. This node describes the shared HCM remodeling endpoint rather than a NEXN-specific finding — no NEXN-specific myocardial histopathology has been reported in the CMH20 families, so the node is marked HYPOTHETICAL for this entry.

evidence.snippet: Two missense mutations, c.391C>G (p.Q131E) and c.835C>T (p.R279C), were identified in exons 5 and 8 of NEXN, respectively, in two probands.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the two HCM probands in whom NEXN missense variants were found, in a cohort screened specifically for HCM.

evidence.snippet: We also detected NEXN variants in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and sudden infant death syndrome/idiopathic ventricular fibrillation, although a causal link could not be established.
evidence.explanation: Independent observation of NEXN variants in HCM patients, but explicitly without establishing causation — hence INDIRECT.

steps/4.description: The defining clinical phenotype: left ventricular hypertrophy not explained by abnormal loading conditions. Reported in two families carrying NEXN missense variants in the original CMH20 report, and in three of 29 NEXN variant-carrying probands in a large French cardiomyopathy sequencing series — though in the latter the authors state a causal link could not be established. Frequency is deliberately omitted: the number of reported carriers is too small, and the gene-disease validity too uncertain, to support a frequency band.

edges/2.description: The steps linking Z-disc destabilization to a hypertrophic (as opposed to dilated) remodeling response have not been established for NEXN; no HCM-recapitulating NEXN model system has been reported.

evidence.snippet: We screened NEXN in 121 unrelated HCM patients who did not carry any mutation in eight genes commonly mutated in myofilament disease.
evidence.explanation: Describes the ascertainment: a sarcomere-gene-negative HCM cohort screened for NEXN, which is the entire clinical basis for the CMH20 designation.

evidence.snippet: Therefore, the mutations in NEXN that we describe here may further expand the knowledge of Z-disc genes in the pathogenesis of HCM.
evidence.explanation: The originating study's own conclusion is hedged ("may further expand"), consistent with the later Limited classification.

evidence.snippet: The majority of genes previously reported as causative of HCM and commonly included in diagnostic tests have limited or no evidence of disease association. Systematically curated HCM genes are essential to guide appropriate reporting of variants and ensure the best possible outcomes for HCM families.

For NEXN specifically, counseling must convey that the NEXN-HCM gene-disease relationship is classified Limited by ClinGen, so a NEXN variant found in an HCM patient generally should not be used for predictive cascade testing or to release genotype-negative relatives from clinical surveillance. Management follows standard nonsyndromic HCM care: symptom-directed pharmacotherapy, arrhythmia surveillance, sudden-death risk stratification with implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement where indicated, and septal reduction therapy for drug-refractory obstruction. Consult the umbrella `Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy` entry and current HCM guidelines for details; this entry deliberately does not restate them.

open_questions/0.rationale: MONDO:0013477 / OMIM 613876 exist as a numbered HCM series entry, but the evidence base has moved against them. ClinGen classifies NEXN-HCM as Limited (2023), and the 2025 multicentre burden study of 60 NEXN carriers found no HCM association while confirming enrichment in DCM/NDLVC. If the association is spurious, this entry should eventually be marked disputed rather than fleshed out with borrowed sarcomeric-HCM mechanism, and NEXN variants should not be reported as causal in HCM diagnostic testing.

evidence.snippet: Loss of nexilin in zebrafish led to perturbed Z-disk stability and heart failure.
evidence.explanation: The canonical nexilin model system produces heart failure in a dilated context, not hypertrophy — the mismatch this discussion records.

open_questions/1.rationale: Every published nexilin model — zebrafish knockdown, mouse knockout — yields dilated cardiomyopathy with endomyocardial/endocardial fibroelastosis, and human NEXN truncating variants segregate with DCM/NDLVC. No animal or iPSC-cardiomyocyte model recapitulating a NEXN-driven hypertrophic phenotype has been reported. The mechanistic chain from Z-disc destabilization to hypertrophic (rather than dilated) remodeling is therefore entirely unmodelled, which is why the downstream nodes in this entry carry mechanism_confidence HYPOTHETICAL and an INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES causal edge.

evidence.snippet: Few clinical data are available on NEXN mutation carriers, and the gene's involvement in cardiomyopathies or sudden death has not been fully established.

open_questions/2.rationale: The published clinical description of CMH20 amounts to two families in the 2010 report plus three probands in a French series whose causality was explicitly not established. No cohort has reported age at onset, hypertrophy distribution, late gadolinium enhancement, outflow gradients, or arrhythmic outcomes specific to NEXN HCM carriers. Consequently no phenotype in this entry carries a `frequency:` band, and the disarray/fibrosis phenotypes are inferred from the HCM disease definition rather than observed in carriers.

evidence.snippet: All IMAGe-associated mutations clustered in the PCNA-binding domain of CDKN1C and resulted in loss of PCNA binding, distinguishing them from the mutations of CDKN1C that cause Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, an overgrowth syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Localizes the variants to one domain and contrasts them with the overgrowth-causing variant class in the same gene.

steps/1.description: A heterozygous missense variant in the PCNA-binding domain of the maternally expressed CDKN1C allele. All IMAGe-associated variants cluster in this domain and abolish PCNA binding, which is what distinguishes them from the Beckwith-Wiedemann variants elsewhere in the same gene.

evidence.snippet: the IMAGe-associated mutant CDKN1C proteins were fairly stable even in the presence of cycloheximide, whereas the wild-type protein was almost completely degraded via the proteasome pathway
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates the stabilization that constitutes the gain of function.

evidence.snippet: loss of PCNA binding and suppression of CDKN1C monoubiquitination by IMAGe-associated mutations hardly explain the reduced-growth phenotype
evidence.explanation: States the explanatory gap that protein stabilization fills, which is why this node sits between the variant and the growth phenotype.

steps/2.description: Wild-type p57KIP2 is short-lived and turned over by the proteasome. IMAGe-associated mutant proteins remain stable in the presence of cycloheximide, so the variant acts by escaping degradation. This is the step that resolves an apparent paradox: loss of PCNA binding alone does not explain undergrowth, but accumulation of a cell-cycle inhibitor does.

evidence.snippet: targeted expression of IMAGe-associated CDKN1C mutations in Drosophila caused severe eye growth defects compared to wild-type CDKN1C, suggesting a gain-of-function mechanism

evidence.snippet: the reduced-growth phenotype of IMAGe syndrome derives from CDKN1C gain-of-function due to IMAGe-associated mutations driving increased protein stability
evidence.explanation: States the causal chain from stabilization to reduced growth that this node asserts.

steps/3.description: CDKN1C inhibits cell-cycle progression, so a stabilized, accumulating protein suppresses proliferation. Targeted expression of IMAGe-associated CDKN1C in Drosophila caused severe eye growth defects relative to wild-type CDKN1C - the in vivo demonstration that the variant is hypermorphic rather than merely non-functional.

genes/0.notes: CDKN1C (11p15.4) encodes p57KIP2, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor. Variants elsewhere in the gene cause Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome by loss of function, so the domain, not merely the gene, is what identifies IMAGe.

evidence.snippet: Sterile alpha motif (SAM) and Src homology-3 (SH3) domain-containing 3 (SASH3), also called SH3-containing lymphocyte protein (SLY1), is a putative adaptor protein that is postulated to play an important role in the organization of signaling complexes and propagation of signal transduction cascades in lymphocytes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes SASH3 as a lymphocyte adaptor whose role is the organisation of signalling complexes, which is the function lost here.

evidence.snippet: Src Homology 3 Domain-containing Adaptor Protein 3 (SASH3) deficiency is an X-linked immune disorder.
evidence.explanation: A later independent group describing the entity in the same terms.

steps/1.description: The initiating lesion. SASH3 is expressed only in lymphocytes and has no enzymatic activity; it is a scaffold whose SH3 and sterile alpha motif domains recruit and connect downstream effectors. Nonsense variants (p.Gln169*, p.Arg245*, p.Arg288*) abolish the protein, and the single reported missense variant, p.Arg347Cys, falls in a conserved motif adjacent to the Ser349 phosphorylation site. Because expression is lymphocyte restricted, the consequences of losing it are confined to the lymphoid compartment rather than being systemic.

evidence.snippet: SASH3 deficiency was described as a novel X-linked combined immunodeficiency with immune dysregulation, associated with impaired TCR signaling and thymocyte survival in humans.
evidence.explanation: States the human signalling defect. The sentence is this case report restating the index cohort's result rather than its own, hence BACKGROUND.

evidence.snippet: SLY1 was recently identified as an X-chromosomal SH3 protein that is serine phosphorylated (Ser27) upon B-and T-cell receptor engagement.
evidence.explanation: Identifies antigen-receptor engagement as the stimulus that modifies the protein, which is the molecular basis for placing it in this pathway. The sentence restates earlier work, so it is marked BACKGROUND.

steps/2.description: Without the SASH3 scaffold, signals initiated at the T-cell and B-cell antigen receptors are not propagated normally. In the mouse the same protein is phosphorylated on Ser27 upon T- or B-cell receptor engagement and shuttles from nucleus to cytoplasm, which is the molecular event this node loses. In patients the readout is abnormal T-cell activation and proliferation, and the defect is corrected by re-expressing SASH3.

evidence.snippet: In vitro T-cell differentiation of CD34+ cells and molecular signatures of rearrangements at the T-cell receptor α (TRA) locus were indicative of impaired thymocyte survival.
evidence.explanation: The human basis for this node. It is an in vitro differentiation assay plus a rearrangement signature, not a thymic biopsy, which is why the staging detail below comes from the mouse.

evidence.snippet: SLY1 was identified as a novel anti-apoptotic protein required for developmental progression of T cell precursors to the CD4+CD8+ double-positive stage by protecting from premature programmed cell death initiation in developing CD4-CD8- double-negative thymocytes.
evidence.explanation: Names the developmental checkpoint and the mechanism of loss in the mouse. It is the source of the staging claim and cannot stand for the human block on its own.

evidence.snippet: Studies of apoptosis and proliferation in SLy1KO thymocytes revealed decreased proliferation in the DN3 subpopulation as a possible reason for the decreased thymocyte number.
evidence.explanation: Adds reduced DN3 proliferation alongside apoptosis as a contributor to the reduced thymocyte number in the mouse.

steps/3.description: Developing thymocytes require the SASH3 scaffold to survive the transition from the CD4-CD8- double-negative to the CD4+CD8+ double-positive stage. In patients this is inferred from in vitro differentiation of CD34+ progenitors and from the rearrangement signature at the T-cell receptor alpha locus, which reports how long thymocytes survive at the double-positive stage. In the mouse the block is direct and staged: thymic cellularity falls by about half and precursors are deleted by premature programmed cell death, with reduced proliferation in the DN3 subpopulation contributing.

evidence.snippet: Patients exhibited CD4+ T-cell lymphopenia, decreased T-cell proliferation, cell cycle progression, and increased T-cell apoptosis in response to mitogens.
evidence.explanation: All three components of this node, measured directly in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: The patient's immunological phenotype included marked B cell lymphopenia with reduced pre-switch and switch memory B cells, decreased CD4+ and CD8+ naïve T cells, elevated CD4+ and CD8+ TEMRA cells, and abnormal T cell activation and proliferation.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation of abnormal T-cell activation and proliferation in a second, unrelated patient.

evidence.snippet: The increased susceptibility of SLy1 knock-out (KO) mice was caused by reduced proliferation of differentiated T cells.
evidence.explanation: The mouse counterpart, which additionally supplies the Foxo1 mechanism the description flags as untested in humans.

steps/4.description: Peripheral T cells that reach the circulation respond poorly to receptor and mitogen stimulation: proliferation is reduced, cell-cycle progression is impaired, and apoptosis is increased. In the mouse the corresponding defect is dysregulated Foxo1 shuttling after T-cell receptor signalling, which raises cell-cycle inhibitor expression and limits clonal expansion; whether the human proliferative defect runs through Foxo1 has not been tested.

evidence.snippet: A shared feature among these cases was a tendency toward reduced lymphocyte subsets, particularly NK cells.
evidence.explanation: The human observation, and marked INDIRECT because of the inference step it needs: the sentence is about the immunodeficiency-gene subset of a congenital-neutropenia cohort as a whole, not about the SASH3 patient in it. SASH3 is named among those genes elsewhere in the same paper, so NK reduction in this disease follows from the cohort statement rather than being asserted by it.

evidence.snippet: Unlike the case for T or B lymphocytes, where SLy1 shuttles between the cytoplasm and nucleus to facilitate signal transduction, in NK cells SLy1 functions as a ribosomal protein and is located solely in the cytoplasm.
evidence.explanation: The reason this node is drawn as a separate branch rather than downstream of the signalling node. In the mouse the NK role is a different molecular function altogether.

evidence.snippet: In brief, we demonstrated that SLy1 is indispensable for adequate numbers of viable, activatable NK cells with an intact cytolytic capacity, and that those phenotypic alterations are p53-mediated.
evidence.explanation: Ties NK number, viability and cytotoxicity to SLy1 loss in the mouse, and attributes them to p53.

steps/5.description: NK cell numbers are reduced in most reported patients, and NK deficiency is a recurring feature of the SASH3 cases ascertained through congenital neutropenia sequencing. The mechanism is the least settled part of this entry. In the mouse, SLy1 in NK cells does not act as a signalling scaffold at all: it stabilises the ribosome, and its loss frees ribosomal proteins, stabilises p53, and drives NK senescence and exhaustion with reduced cytotoxicity. Whether human SASH3 has the same non-signalling role in NK cells has not been tested, so the mouse mechanism is recorded here but not asserted of patients.

evidence.snippet: Immunohistochemistry performed after clinically indicated splenectomy revealed severe hypoplasia/absence of germinal centres.
evidence.explanation: The only direct human histological observation of the germinal centre in this disease, and the reason this node is placed at the germinal centre rather than downstream of it.

evidence.snippet: However, further analysis of B cells demonstrated a considerable reduction in IgM memory B cells (CD19+CD27+IgD+) at 1.6% and switched memory B cells (CD19+CD27+IgD−) at 2.4%
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the memory B-cell loss in a patient whose total B-cell count and IgG were normal, separating the germinal-centre output defect from B-cell lymphopenia.

evidence.snippet: Sly1(d/d) mice exhibit reduced lymphoid organ sizes, diminished marginal zone B-cell numbers, and severely impaired antibody responses against T-dependent and -independent antigens.
evidence.explanation: The mouse humoral phenotype. It supports the T-dependent antibody failure but is a marginal-zone rather than a germinal-centre lesion, so it is supporting rather than defining evidence here.

evidence.snippet: Consistent with the loss of MZ B cells, the production of antigen-specific IgM antibodies following immunization with pneumococcal polysaccharides was severely impaired in Sly1(d/d) mice.
evidence.explanation: The mouse counterpart of the poor polysaccharide vaccine response reported in the adult patient with a common-variable-immunodeficiency-like presentation.

steps/6.description: The humoral arm fails at the germinal centre. Splenic histology in one patient, examined after a clinically indicated splenectomy, showed severe hypoplasia or absence of germinal centres. Patients consistently lose class-switched and IgM memory B cells even when total B-cell numbers and IgG are preserved, and serum IgM is frequently low. In the Sly1 mutant mouse the corresponding defect is a selective block at the marginal-zone B-cell transition with severely impaired antibody responses to both T-dependent and T-independent antigens.

evidence.snippet: Here, we identified 3 novel SASH3 deleterious variants in 4 unrelated male patients with a history of combined immunodeficiency and immune dysregulation that manifested as recurrent sinopulmonary, cutaneous, and mucosal infections and refractory autoimmune cytopenias.
evidence.explanation: Refractory autoimmune cytopenias in the index cohort, alongside the infectious picture.

evidence.snippet: We studied a patient with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia and identified a germline mutation in SASH3 (c.862C>T;p.Arg288Ter), indicating a recently identified IEI.
evidence.explanation: A patient in whom the autoimmune cytopenias were the presenting illness and the immunodeficiency was found afterwards.

steps/7.description: Immune dysregulation is a defining half of this disease rather than an incidental complication. Patients develop refractory autoimmune cytopenias, and in the one case studied in detail the autoimmune phenotype came with reduced regulatory T cells, T-cell exhaustion, and an expanded CD21low T-bet+ CD11c+ population. How loss of a lymphocyte adaptor produces loss of tolerance is not established; the thymocyte selection defect and the regulatory T-cell deficit are both plausible routes and neither has been tested against the other in patients.

evidence.snippet: These findings define a new type of X-linked combined immunodeficiency in humans that recapitulates many of the abnormalities reported in mice with Sly1-/- and Sly1Δ/Δ mutations, highlighting an important role of SASH3 in human lymphocyte function and survival.
evidence.explanation: The defining statement that this is a combined immunodeficiency.

steps/8.description: Both the cellular and the humoral arms are affected, which is why the 2022 IUIS classification places SASH3 deficiency in the table of immunodeficiencies affecting cellular and humoral immunity. Severity ranges from a presentation indistinguishable from common variable immunodeficiency to refractory autoimmune cytopenias, and one variant carrier is asymptomatic.

evidence.snippet: Here, we identified 3 novel SASH3 deleterious variants in 4 unrelated male patients with a history of combined immunodeficiency and immune dysregulation that manifested as recurrent sinopulmonary, cutaneous, and mucosal infections and refractory autoimmune cytopenias.
evidence.explanation: Recurrent sinopulmonary infection in all four index patients.

steps/9.description: Recurrent upper and lower respiratory tract infection is the commonest presenting complaint, and in the adult case bilateral influenza A pneumonia was one of the two episodes that prompted genetic testing.

evidence.snippet: Here, we identified 3 novel SASH3 deleterious variants in 4 unrelated male patients with a history of combined immunodeficiency and immune dysregulation that manifested as recurrent sinopulmonary, cutaneous, and mucosal infections and refractory autoimmune cytopenias.
evidence.explanation: Cutaneous infection named alongside the sinopulmonary and mucosal infections.

evidence.snippet: Two separate, severe viral infections drew our attention and pointed to an underlying T cell defect: severe varicella zoster virus (VZV) infection at the age of 4 years and bilateral pneumonia due type A influenza infection at the age of 38.
evidence.explanation: The single reported episode and the inference the authors drew from it.

steps/11.description: Reported in one adult patient at four years of age. It is recorded here because it is the observation that redirected a long-standing common variable immunodeficiency diagnosis toward an underlying T-cell defect, not because severe VZV is an established feature of the disease; a single case cannot establish that.

evidence.snippet: Patients exhibited CD4+ T-cell lymphopenia, decreased T-cell proliferation, cell cycle progression, and increased T-cell apoptosis in response to mitogens.
evidence.explanation: CD4+ T-cell lymphopenia in the index cohort.

steps/12.description: The most consistent laboratory abnormality in this disease, present in the index cohort and in every later case in which lymphocyte subsets were reported.

evidence.snippet: SASH3 deficiency is typically characterized by three main findings: cytopenia affecting one or more blood cell lineages (including white blood cells such as neutrophils and lymphocytes, red blood cells or platelets), hypogammaglobulinemia and reduced numbers of lymphocyte subsets (T cells, B cells or NK cells)
evidence.explanation: Summarises reduced lymphocyte subsets, T cells included, as one of the three characteristic findings across the reported cases.

steps/13.description: Both CD4+ and CD8+ compartments are affected, so total T-cell numbers are reduced as well as the CD4+ subset.

evidence.snippet: Patients exhibited CD4+ T-cell lymphopenia, decreased T-cell proliferation, cell cycle progression, and increased T-cell apoptosis in response to mitogens.

evidence.snippet: These patients also manifested neutropenia and B-cell and natural killer (NK)-cell lymphopenia.

evidence.snippet: We studied a patient with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia and identified a germline mutation in SASH3 (c.862C>T;p.Arg288Ter), indicating a recently identified IEI.
